The 15s buys nothing on this path. readHeader opens a FRESH connection per file, so a timeout does not trigger reconnect-and-continue — it skips the file and moves on, with the retry scheduler picking it up later. A read that has not returned in 5 seconds on a local gigabit NAS is not slow, it is dead. The probe harness was dropped to 3s on exactly this reasoning.

DELIBERATELY HELD until the retry changes land: the correct value depends on failures carrying a reason and the user being able to retry deliberately, so changing the number now would move it without the structure that makes it correct. Note the skip rate also drifted upward during the run — roughly 2.8% over files 900-1400 rising to 5.5% by 2100 — which may indicate the NAS degrading under sustained load and would argue for pacing as well as a shorter ceiling.

DONE 2026-08-01. readHeader 15s -> 5s, as a named constant with the measurement recorded in the comment. Held until the ledger landed because the correct value depended on failures carrying a reason; now a timeout is recorded as kind .timeout, does NOT consume a retry attempt, and is retried on a fresh connection.

Verified on the phase 2 device run: 6 timeouts, all six recovered on retry attempt 2. A clean 159-file scan went 91.9s -> 58.5s. The long wait bought nothing on this path — readHeader opens a fresh connection per file, so a timeout does not trigger reconnect-and-continue, it records the failure and moves on.

features.name: Log retention, multi-file rotation, and export destinations
features.desc:
Agreed 2026-07-31, three parts. (1) MULTI-FILE ROTATION — keep the last several rotations rather than a single prev file, so a long run stays fully recoverable. maxBytes was raised 256KB -> 8MB for the full-library scan, which is a deliberate trade for the current phase rather than a permanent default. (2) ARCHIVE EXPORT — bundle every rotation into one zip (ZIPFoundation is already a dependency for DB backup) offered to both the share sheet AND the NAS, because a user cannot currently reach even the single rotated file: logFileURL returns only the current log. (3) VERBOSITY LEVELS — an 11,670-file scan does not need a resolveAlbum line per album at normal verbosity; most of the volume is per-album detail that only matters when investigating.

Writing to the share on demand after a run, not continuously during it: per-line SMB writes would consume the connection budget and fail exactly when diagnostics matter. Same destination and reasoning as fScanReportShareExport.

features.name: Retry pass restarts from the first album rather than resuming mid-pass
features.desc:
The artwork retry pass has no per-album progress marker within a pass, so an interruption restarts it from album 1, re-attempting albums it already handled. Cheap at a handful of albums and self-limiting via embeddedArtRetryCount, but it is the same gap bArtworkPassNotResumable closed for the scan's own artwork passes. Subsumed by fScanSessionLedger, which makes retry part of the session and therefore resumable by construction.

FIXED 2026-08-01, subsumed by the ledger. Verified directly on device: retry killed mid-file resumed reporting '1 pending', not the full queue of 6.

features.name: Foreground change check runs artwork passes and retry scheduler even when nothing changed
features.desc:
A change check that filters to zero files still runs all three artwork passes, the retry scheduler, and the full state transition sequence. Harmless in wall-clock terms — measured 16.9s on an 11,670-file library, most of which is the walk — but it is ceremony for nothing, and it is what widens the window for bPhantomScanInterruptedDialog by setting scanState 'scanning' on every foreground. Observed 2026-07-31.

RAISED FROM LOW TO HIGH, 2026-08-08. This entry called the cost 'harmless in wall-clock terms', which was assessed before anyone connected it to the screen never locking. runScan sets isIdleTimerDisabled = true, and this pipeline runs on EVERY foreground — so ~16.9s on Tom's library is not merely wasted work, it is seventeen seconds of suppressed auto-lock every single time the app is opened, paid in battery and screen burn.

It is also the exposure surface for bAutoLockNeverRestored: that latch only bites when a pipeline run fails to reach its end, and this is what makes runs frequent. Removing the unnecessary work removes most of the opportunity. Fix them together.

features.name: Unit tests for the scan session ledger
features.desc:
BUILT AND VERIFIED 2026-08-01. 20 tests in SorrivaTests/ScanLedgerTests.swift, green, running in ~37s.

They run the REAL SMBScanner against a real directory of real FLAC files through SorrivaDatabase.shared. LedgerTestFixtures synthesizes structurally valid FLAC — fLaC magic, STREAMINFO carrying sample rate and total samples so duration parses, VORBIS_COMMENT with tags — and the byte arithmetic was verified against parseVorbisComment's exact indexing before the fixtures were written. A fixture returning canned metadata would pass whether or not the parser worked.

FixtureMediaSourceReader gained beforeRead/beforeList hooks and call counters. cancelScanAfterReads(n) simulates a kill by cancelling the enclosing task, which is what the scan loop actually checks; failReadNumber(n) simulates a bad read, which the scanner catches and records. Conflating those two produced two false failures on the first run and is documented in both files — a read failure is recorded and the scan continues, only cancellation leaves rows planned.

Seventeen tests drive a real scan: plan matches disk, audit totals, resume works the remainder without replanning, session id survives, timeout does not consume an attempt while a content failure does, mtime detects a tag edit with size held constant, deletion reconciles and stays source-scoped. Three more construct known-bad ledger state directly and assert the DETECTION machinery — unaccounted rows are found AND named, audit arithmetic is exact, per-folder rollup splits correctly and omits clean folders. Those three need no scan and run in ~0.02s each.

TESTED THE TESTS. Per Tom: 'test end to end until working, build unit tests, then test the tests.' The success-path recordLedgerOutcome was commented out and the suite rerun: 10 red, 10 green. All three detection tests stayed green (they write their own rows and never touch the scanner), both resume tests and all the audit tests went red, and the failures were specific rather than cascading. Reverted, all 20 green again. The suite is not passing vacuously.

Note testPlanMatchesFilesOnDisk correctly PASSED under the mutation — it asserts the total across all buckets, and the rows still existed, just stranded at 'planned'. testCleanScanLeavesNothingUnaccounted is what catches that.

features.name: Retry scheduler reports art pending when the ledger says zero
features.desc:
ScanRetryScheduler's completion line reads albumsNeedingEmbeddedArtRetry(), a pre-v18 fallback selecting on embeddedArtFailed. Since artwork moved into the ledger that query is a second opinion, and it disagrees: every run ends with 'LEDGER: artwork — ... unaccounted 0' immediately followed by 'scheduler COMPLETE — 1 art still pending'. The ledger is correct.

This is the last artwork path not reading the ledger, and it is the same class of problem the ledger was built to remove — two sources of truth for one question. Cosmetic today in that no work is actually lost, but it will confuse anyone reading the log, and it is exactly the kind of disagreement that hid real bugs before.

FIX: report from scanSessionAudit(sessionId:kind: .artwork) when a ledger session exists, falling back to the old query only when it does not. While in there, re-read the other two callers (ScanCoordinator.hasOutstandingWork and ScanRetryScheduler.queuesClear) to confirm neither fallback can fire while a ledger session exists — if one ever wins over the ledger, a session can report outstanding work that is not real, which is how a scan gets stuck.

VERIFY: the 'scheduler COMPLETE' line must agree with the 'LEDGER: artwork' line immediately above it. Observed on every run of the 2026-08-01 regression.

features.name: Two session identifiers for one concept
features.desc:
There were two: a scan sessionId used for the folder_stats stamp and the log tag, and a separate ledger session id used for the audit. Different UUIDs for the same thing, so the log said one and the audit said another — visible 2026-08-01 as a scan tagged D60CE953 whose retry was tagged 107962AD, same run.

Tom rejected a one-line fix that would have made the tag agree, on the grounds that two identifiers for one thing is the same duplication the ledger exists to remove. FIXED by collapsing them: runScan now creates or resumes the ledger session BEFORE binding the log tag, and that id serves the ledger, the folder_stats stamp, currentScanSessionId and the tag. The ledger id wins because it is the durable one — scan_sessions survives a kill and is recoverable via activeScanSession, whereas currentScanSessionId is cleared at pipeline completion.

features.name: Concurrent scans overwrote each other's log session tag
features.desc:
ScanLogSession held a single global `current`, so a second scan calling begin() while the first was still in its artwork phase overwrote the first scan's tag. The 2026-08-01 phase 1 log shows it in three separate runs where the id changes partway through, plus the LEDGER: artwork line coming out untagged entirely.

The ledger was correct throughout; only the log became unsearchable, which defeats the one property fScanSessionLogCorrelation exists to provide. FIXED with @TaskLocal — scoped to the task and its children, so concurrent pipelines cannot interfere by construction. Bound around the whole run and rebound inside the detached pipeline task, since Task.detached deliberately does not inherit task-locals. A global `ambient` remains as a fallback for log calls made outside any bound task.

Separately, 'LEDGER: ' had been omitted from taggedPrefixes when LEDGER was introduced as a category, so those lines were never tagged regardless of scope. Tom: 'the ledger can't wait that long. it is the summary of the audit.'

features.name: Four pre-existing test failures leave the suite red
features.desc:
As of 2026-08-01 the full suite runs 66 tests with 4 failures, none from the ledger work (ScanLedgerTests is 20/20 green). Known: AlbumGenreTests.testRescanReplacesGenresRatherThanAccumulating fails with expected ["Rock"] but got ["Synth-Pop"] — rescanning is not replacing the album's genre set. Three more, one each in a 2-test, 3-test and 16-test suite, not yet identified.

This matters beyond the individual bugs: a suite that is red by default trains everyone to ignore it, and then a real regression hides in the noise. The ledger suite's value is materially reduced by sitting inside a red overall run. Identify all four and either fix them or mark them explicitly as expected failures with a reason.

features.name: Catalogue the library data-quality issues seen in the full scan - currently anecdotal
features.desc:
PLACEHOLDER, deliberately. Tom observed several data-quality problems during the 11,670-file full-library scan. None were catalogued, none were investigated, and the library has since been dropped — so they cannot be re-derived by looking. This entry exists so the BACKLOG is recorded even though its contents are not.

OBSERVED, ANECDOTALLY — Tom's words: 'albums broken out over multiple entries, missing art, etc. never cataloged and never investigated so they are anecdotal at the moment.' Also unknown: how MULTI-DISC albums are handled, which needs the raw folder structure examined before anything can be said about it. Albums splitting into multiple entries and multi-disc handling may well be the same problem — a disc-per-folder layout producing one album row per folder — but that is a hypothesis, not a finding.

TREAT AS UNVERIFIED. None of the above has been reproduced or measured. Acting on any of it before reproducing it would repeat the mistake that closed PlaybackStore phase C, where a behaviour was recorded as a defect from reading code rather than measuring, and three rounds of fixes were built on a wrong premise. Each item needs a repro against real files before it becomes a bug.

FIRST STEP is not a fix. Rescan a library, then catalogue what is actually wrong with evidence — specific albums, specific tags, specific folder layouts — and split THAT into real defects. The scan-session ledger already accounts for every file, so the raw material for an audit exists; what is missing is a pass over the RESULT rather than the process.

Related existing items, which may turn out to be facets of this: bDuplicateAlbumDetection, bArtworkArtistQuery, fArtworkManualSearchUtility, fMusicBrainzCoverArt.

features.name: SMBClient crashes reading past the end of a short response buffer
features.desc:
HARD CRASH, caught in the debugger 2026-08-06 during a scan in the iOS Simulator. EXC_BREAKPOINT in SMBClient/Sources/SMBClient/ByteReader.swift:24:

    func read(count: Int) -> Data {
        let value = data[offset..<(offset + count)]   // count = 64

A range out of bounds: it slices 64 bytes when fewer remain, so offset + count exceeds data.count. The class even exposes `availableBytes` (data.count - offset) and does not consult it. 64 bytes is an SMB2 header, so this is the library parsing a response that arrived short or empty.

CALL PATH: Connection.receive(completion:) -> Connection.receive(upTo:completion:) -> ByteReader.read() -> ByteReader.read(count:), on a utility-QoS worker thread, beneath SMBMediaSourceReader.readHeader.

WE MAY BE CAUSING IT. MediaSourceReader force-cancels a hung connection on timeout via session.disconnect() -> NWConnection.cancel(), which is deliberate and documented (it is THE fix for connection exhaustion). But cancelling a connection mid-read is exactly what hands ByteReader a truncated buffer. So our timeout may be triggering the library's missing bounds check. That is a hypothesis from the stack, not a proven sequence.

AFFECTS THE PHONE TOO — nothing here is simulator-specific. It has simply never been seen, because on device a crash looks like the app disappearing rather than pausing in a debugger. Worth re-reading past 'the app closed during a scan' reports in that light.

WHY IT SURFACED NOW: the simulator work. A device build hands you a crash log after the fact; the simulator paused on the faulting line with the buffer state visible. This is the first defect found purely because the app was running somewhere inspectable.

MISLEADING SYMPTOM, worth recording: the app appears HUNG, not crashed. kill -9 does not work and simctl shutdown never completes, because lldb holds the process. Do not chase it as a hang — check Xcode first.

OPTIONS: guard the read (fork or patch SMBClient), or avoid handing it a truncated buffer by reordering our cancellation. Needs the actual sequence established before choosing. Sample and screenshot from the session are the evidence.

features.name: Pre-v21 keychain entries keyed by share id are never cleaned up
features.desc:
deleteLibrarySource / deleteLibrarySourcesByHost are a bare DELETE FROM library_sources and never touch KeychainCredentialStore. The credential entry survives, keyed to a sourceId that no longer exists — unreachable by any code path, and one more accumulates per removed share.

OBSERVED 2026-08-06 in the simulator: the test share was removed, and the NAS password remained in the simulator keychain afterwards.

WHY IT MATTERS BEYOND TIDINESS: it is a credential the user believes they removed. 'Remove Share' says it deletes the share and all scanned tracks; a reasonable person reads that as removing what the app stored about that server. Leaving the password behind is a privacy expectation broken quietly, and it is the kind of thing that reads badly in an App Store review of a music app that asks for NAS credentials.

FIX: delete the keychain entry alongside the row. Note deleteLibrarySourcesByHost removes several sources at once, so it needs the ids before the DELETE, not after.

Pairs with bNoCredentialReuseOnReAddingServer — together they mean the password is both kept when it should not be, and unusable when it would help.

NARROWED 2026-08-07. The lifecycle question is settled: removing a SHARE now keeps credentials deliberately (you may add another share on that server a minute later), and removing a SERVER forgets them, which is the only unambiguous statement of intent. What remains is narrower and cosmetic — the v21 migration re-files additively rather than moving, so entries written under the old sourceId key persist. They are inert and unreachable. Cleaning them up means deleting keychain items on the strength of a migration having succeeded, which is exactly the risk v21 was written to avoid, so this is Low and may reasonably stay open forever.

features.name: Re-adding a server always asks for credentials again, even though they were saved
features.desc:
AddSMBSourceView only ever WRITES credentials — the single KeychainCredentialStore reference in the file is a set(). Nothing looks up an existing credential for a host, so adding a share on a server already authenticated to always prompts for username and password.

TOM'S OBSERVATION, 2026-08-06, and the diagnosis follows it: 'why isn't this pulling credentials from keychain. i asked for them to be saved. in the app on my phone, the credentials are preloaded. not 100% sure if that is the case if all shares are removed though.' Exactly right. On the phone they appear preloaded because a source ROW still exists and the UI populates from it. Remove every share for that server and the link is gone — there is no lookup by host to fall back on. Not a simulator difference; the phone behaves identically once the last share is removed.

USER IMPACT: re-adding a share means retyping a NAS password the app was explicitly asked to save. Also relevant to mounting a SECOND share on the same server — that flow has the credentials already and should not ask twice.

FIX: look up an existing credential by host and pre-fill, with the user able to override. Depends on keychain entries being addressable by host rather than only by sourceId, which is worth checking — and on bKeychainOrphanedOnShareDelete, since stale entries must not be offered for a server whose shares were deliberately removed.

FIXED 2026-08-07. Credentials were keyed by the share's sourceId, so removing the LAST share on a server orphaned them under a key nothing could look up again — re-adding minted a fresh UUID, missed, and asked for a password the app was still holding. Adding a second share to a SURVIVING server worked, because a live source row was there to read from, which is why it looked intermittent. Now keyed per server (CredentialKey.forHost — lowercased, trailing .local stripped, so AV-Server and av-server.local are one server). Migration v21 re-files ADDITIVELY, leaving old entries in place: a half-finished keychain move would lock a user out of their own NAS with no recovery, and resolvedCredentials' fallback tier still answers from the old key. Verified end to end on the simulator: migration re-filed, a change check logged into the NAS and completed, the share was removed, re-added, and the credentials screen came up prefilled and authenticated with nothing typed.

features.name: Remove Share cleans up less than Clear Local Library — two paths, one more thorough
features.desc:
Measured 2026-08-06 before and after removing the test share: tracks 95 -> 0, albums 8 -> 0, sources 1 -> 0, artists 41 -> 41.

THE POINT IS THE COMPARISON, not the orphaned rows on their own. SorrivaDatabase.clearLocalLibrary() — behind Settings > Clear Local Library — deletes track_artists, artist_albums, tracks, albums, ARTISTS, folder_stats and scan_skips, AND removes cached artwork files, AND resets the sources' scan state while keeping the sources themselves. Remove Share deletes the source row and its tracks and albums, and stops there.

Two paths expressing the same intent — forget this indexed media — with one materially more thorough. That is drift rather than a decision, and the fix is to have Remove Share go through the same cleanup scoped to one source rather than maintain a second, weaker implementation.

Also leaves cached artwork files behind, which clearLocalLibrary explicitly deletes with the comment 'prevents orphaned files accumulating after each clear'. Same reasoning applies here and was not applied.

SEPARATE DESIGN QUESTION, ANSWERED: Tom asked whether stations should be dropped too — 'shouldn't you go back to a zero media saved?' Concluded no, and no change made. Both operations are about the LOCAL library; stations are a different service and survive correctly. A true factory reset including stations would be a distinct action and does not exist today.

features.name: Share track count under-reports by the number of tracks retry recovered
features.desc:
The UI showed '93 tracks' while the database held 95 rows. The difference is exactly the 2 tracks the retry pass resolved: library_sources.trackCount is stamped at the end of the main pass and never updated when retry succeeds. Ledger for the same scan: written 101, resolved 2.

So the count is wrong by precisely the number of files the retry machinery rescued — the one number that most directly demonstrates the retry working. On an 11.6k library where retry recovered 419 files, the shortfall would be substantial and would look like the scan having silently lost tracks.

FIX: recompute trackCount after the retry pass completes, or derive it rather than caching it. Found 2026-08-06 by comparing the app's displayed count with its own database.

CLEAN REPRO AND A PRIORITY BUMP, 2026-08-08. A full auto-scan of the 95-file test share finished with the tracks table holding 95 rows across 8 albums and every planned file accounted for — while library_sources.trackCount read 91. Four files timed out during the walk, the retry pass recovered them, and the denormalised count was never updated afterwards. Exactly what this entry describes, now reproducible on demand.

RAISED FROM MEDIUM TO HIGH because fAutoScanOnShareAdd changed who reads it. The share row is now the primary surface: scans start on their own, so the user's first sight of the result is that row rather than a scan report they watched. A count that is quietly four short is worse than one that is obviously missing — nothing prompts you to doubt it.

features.name: Scan automatically when a share is added, with somewhere to watch and pause it
features.desc:
Adding a share has exactly one purpose — getting its music into the library — so the confirmation dialog asks a question with only one sensible answer. Roon calls this Storage and never makes you kick off a scan of a source you just added; the only actions are disable, edit and delete. Do the same: the scan starts on save, with no prompt.

The blocker is that this is not just deleting the dialog. The dialog carries real information — a large library takes hours, the app must stay in the foreground, and auto-lock is suppressed while it runs. That warning has to move somewhere the user can actually see it, which means a place to watch the scan and pause it. That UI does not exist yet, which is why this is logged rather than built.

A modal shown once and dismissed in five seconds is a worse home for that warning than a progress view that is true the whole time the scan runs. The scan ledger already survives interruption — it resumed cleanly through a hard crash on 2026-08-06 — so pausing and resuming is safe.

This supersedes bScanConfirmDialogLostDuringAddNavigation: with no dialog there is nothing to lose. Manual rescan should survive as a recovery action, demoted rather than primary.

RELOOKED 2026-08-08, after fStorageAndLibraryRestructure settled where things live. This entry said the progress view had to go 'somewhere the user can actually see it' and could not say where, because at the time there was nowhere. THE ANSWER IS THE SHARE ROW IN STORAGE. The share is the unit; its scan is its state; progress belongs on the row alongside track count and last-scanned, not on a separate screen the user has to go looking for. That also means the foreground and auto-lock warning has a permanent home rather than a modal moment.

TWO DIFFERENT THINGS WERE BEING CALLED RESUME. What exists today is CRASH RECOVERY — the ledger reconciles a scan that died and picks up where it stopped, proven through a hard crash on 2026-08-06. What does not exist is DELIBERATE PAUSE AND RESUME: a user stopping a scan because they want their phone back, and restarting it later on purpose. The ledger makes the second safe but does not provide it — pause is a control, and there is no control. Both are needed and they are not the same feature.

Manual rescan stays as a recovery action, demoted rather than primary — a row that scans itself on add and reports its own progress makes 'Scan Now' something you reach for when something looks wrong, not the normal path.

DONE 2026-08-08. scanNewSource now calls confirmAndScanSource directly instead of setting a pending flag for an alert. Verified end to end in the simulator: share removed, re-added, and Save went straight to 'Scanning library…' with no dialog anywhere — and nothing typed, because the credential re-keying earlier the same day (bNoCredentialReuseOnReAddingServer) prefills on re-add. Finished at 95 tracks across 8 albums with every planned file accounted for, including four that timed out and were recovered by the retry pass.

The hours / foreground / auto-lock warning moved into ScanStatusPanel, where it reads 'Keep Sorriva open — backgrounding pauses the scan. Auto-lock is off until it finishes.' True for the whole scan rather than for the five seconds a modal is on screen, which was always the better home for it.

MANUAL RESCAN KEPT ITS CONFIRMATION. Re-reading an already-scanned share IS a question worth asking, and the ••• → Scan Now path is not the one the alert broke on — the defect was specific to the add-share navigation. This supersedes bScanConfirmDialogLostDuringAddNavigation on the path that was broken while leaving the working path alone.

DELIBERATE PAUSE AND RESUME IS STILL NOT BUILT, and is the remaining half. What exists is crash recovery: a stopped or killed scan lands in 'scanning' state and the next foreground offers Scan Incomplete → Resume / Start Over / Cancel, resuming from the ledger. What does not exist is a Stop control, so an auto-started scan currently cannot be halted except by force-quitting. Acceptable on a 95-file test library; not on 11,670. See fScanPauseAndResume.

features.name: Mark a share's albums and tracks unavailable when the app can see the share is offline
features.desc:
A manual disable switch is only worth having if it makes the tracks unavailable in the library, rather than letting the user tap play and get an error on a path that is temporarily gone. And the user should not have to set it — the app can tell that a share is unreachable and mark its albums and tracks unavailable itself. Derived state, not a flag someone has to remember to flip.

The catch that must not be rediscovered: the phone is not in the audio path. Sonos pulls local files straight from the NAS over x-file-cifs, so 'my phone cannot reach the NAS' and 'this music cannot play' are different facts. On cellular away from home the phone can reach nothing, while the speakers at home play that library perfectly. Deriving availability from what the phone can reach would grey out the entire local library every time the user leaves the house, and break remote control of home playback.

So the rule is conditional. On the home network: probe the share, and if it is unreachable mark its albums and tracks unavailable. Off the home network: mark nothing — there is no evidence, and the speakers most likely do have access; let a failed play be the rare fallback.

Two details that decide whether it is pleasant or irritating. Hysteresis: several consecutive failures to go unavailable, one success to come back, so a two-second Wi-Fi hiccup does not grey out eleven thousand tracks. And dim rather than hide — a library that vanishes reads as data loss. The play control should be disabled rather than tappable-then-failing, since stopping the error is the entire point.

This removes the need for a manual disable action altogether, leaving edit and delete. Mostly presentation work, so it belongs with the Storage/Library restructure rather than ahead of it.

features.name: Scan confirmation dialog is destroyed by the add-share navigation, so a new share is never scanned
features.desc:
Adding a share queues a scan and raises a confirmation alert, but the alert appears for under a second and dies untouched — so the share is added and never scanned. Manual rescan from the share menu works, which is the only reason the condition is survivable.

Measured on 2026-08-06 in the simulator. The add flow pops the add screen and pushes the share detail screen 0.1s later, and the detail view is created twice 43ms apart during that transition. The alert was bound to a @State flag on that view, so it went down with the instance that owned it.

Binding the alert to the coordinator instead was tried and did not fix it, for a reason worth recording: SwiftUI does not merely drop the presentation when the host view churns, it writes false back into whatever the alert is bound to. The setter read that as a user dismissal and cleared the queued scan — the same failure with a different victim, and slightly worse, because it also removed the accidental recovery where the pending scan re-raised the alert on a later visit to the screen.

Any real fix needs two things: a setter that ignores false, since a SwiftUI alert cannot be dismissed except by a button, and a host view that is not being rebuilt mid-presentation. Superseded by fAutoScanOnShareAdd — with the scan starting automatically there is no dialog to lose, which is a better outcome than making this one survive a navigation transition.

features.name: A share with no folder fingerprints is treated as never scanned, so it silently stops updating
features.desc:
With folder_stats empty but scanState='complete', lastScanned set and 95 tracks present, the foreground change check logs "AV-Server never scanned — skipping change check" and returns. It does this on every foreground, forever. The share never picks up a new album, and the UI says the scan is complete, so nothing on screen suggests anything is wrong.

The guard at ScanCoordinator.swift:337 is deliberate and its reasoning is sound — with no folder_stats there is nothing to diff against, so every folder would look new and a foreground event would kick off a full initial import the user never asked for (bAutoScanTriggeredOnNeverScannedSource). The defect is the PROXY, not the intent: emptiness of folder_stats is used to mean "never scanned", while lastScanned, scanState and trackCount all say otherwise. Four fields describe one fact and one of them outvotes the other three.

HONEST PROVENANCE: this state was produced ARTIFICIALLY, by deleting folder_stats from the test baseline while trying to mutation-test the rescan guard. No natural path to it has been found, so this is latent rather than observed in the wild. It is logged anyway because the failure is silent and permanent — a library that quietly stops updating is the kind of thing discovered months later, by which point the cause is unrecoverable. Backup & Restore is the first place to look for a real path, since restoring an older or partial database is the obvious way to end up with tracks but no fingerprints.

Likely fix: decide "has been scanned" from lastScanned or trackCount rather than from folder_stats, and when the fingerprints are missing but the library is populated, rebuild them from what is already known instead of either rescanning everything or doing nothing. Found by the scan regression suite (fHarnessRegressionScripts) on its first run.

features.name: Record where each album's artwork came from, and how confident the match was
features.desc:
The artwork review list in fArtworkManualSearchUtility needs to rank albums by doubt, and the data to do that is only half present.

WHAT EXISTS: artManualOverride identifies user-set art. artMatchedName/artMatchedArtist/artMatchScore (v22, 2026-08-07) identify an accepted ONLINE match and how well it scored. artworkWidth/artworkHeight (v15) give the resolution axis for free.

WHAT IS MISSING, confirmed by reading ArtworkBestWins.selectWinner on 2026-08-07: nothing records WHICH PASS WON. The embeddedArtScanned / folderArtScanned / onlineArtAttempted markers say which passes RAN, not which one supplied the image that is on screen. Folder art and embedded art are indistinguishable from each other after the fact. A single artSource value (embedded / folder / online / manual) written wherever the winner is stored closes that.

ALSO MISSING: confidence is persisted only when a match is ACCEPTED. When ArtworkLookup declines — Johnny Cash '18 Greatest Hits' scored 0.40 against a 0.62 bar — the number goes to the debug log and nowhere else. Storing the best rejected score lets the review list say 'we looked and found nothing better than 0.40', which is far more useful than a silent blank, and tells the user the difference between 'never attempted' and 'attempted and nothing was good enough'.

Small, and worth doing BEFORE the maintenance UI rather than during it, so the UI can be built against real data instead of inferring provenance from markers that do not mean what they look like they mean.

DONE 2026-08-08, schema v23. Two columns.

artSource (embedded | folder | online | manual) records WHICH PASS supplied the image on screen. Nothing did before: ArtworkBestWins.selectWinner returns a winner and the caller stores the image, but which pass produced it was thrown away, and the embeddedArtScanned / folderArtScanned / onlineArtAttempted markers record which passes RAN — a different question. Folder art and embedded art were indistinguishable after the fact. Set at all four write sites: the online path in ArtworkCache, the folder and embedded passes in ScanCoordinator, and the embedded retry in ScanRetryScheduler.

artBestRejectedScore records that the online pass LOOKED AND DECLINED. Johnny Cash '18 Greatest Hits' scoring 0.40 against a 0.62 bar used to go to the debug log and nowhere else, so an empty slot could not be told from one never attempted. Verified populated at 0.4 on that exact album, alongside artSource=online and 1200x1200 on an album that did match.

EXISTING ALBUMS SHOW NULL artSource until rescanned, and that is the honest outcome — the information was never recorded, so there is nothing to backfill. Inferring 'online' from a non-null artMatchedName would cover exactly one album and give the rest a false appearance of being known.

features.name: Online artwork is stored at 600x600 when 1200x1200 is available for free
features.desc:
ArtworkCache hardcodes a 600x600 request by substituting into the artworkUrl100 the iTunes API returns. Measured 2026-08-07 across five albums: four served a full 1200x1200 from the same URL — four times the pixels, for the same single request. Only one older asset (Miles Davis, Kind of Blue) genuinely caps at 600.

Request the larger size, then record what actually came back rather than assuming: the response silently returns the largest available, so an asset that caps at 600 yields 600 and must be stored as 600. ImageDimensionReader already measures real dimensions, and artworkWidth/artworkHeight (v15) already store them, so the honest value is available without extra work — and best-wins comparisons depend on those numbers being true.

Matters beyond looking better on a phone: it is the cheapest possible answer to the low-resolution artwork problem, it reduces how much the eventual upscaling work has to do, and on iPad and any future larger display the difference between 600 and 1200 is visible rather than theoretical.

DONE 2026-08-08. The full-size request moved from 600x600 to 1200x1200 — the size is a path component Apple honours up to whatever the asset holds, so this is the same single request for four times the pixels. Verified on a real album: Depeche Mode 'Remixes 81-04' went from 450x450 to 1200x1200.

THE DIMENSIONS ARE NOW MEASURED, NOT ASSUMED, which was the non-obvious half. downloadAndSave returns the true pixel size read by ImageDimensionReader instead of the caller writing the number it asked for. Apple silently returns something smaller when an asset caps out — an older Miles Davis cover genuinely stops at 600 — so recording the REQUESTED size would write a number that is sometimes a lie, and artworkWidth/artworkHeight feed the best-wins comparison. A folder cover that is genuinely larger has to be able to win.

features.name: Artwork of last resort — additional sources, and on-device upscaling for poor originals
features.desc:
Two distinct problems get conflated as 'bad artwork', and they need different answers.

PROBLEM ONE — NO ARTWORK EXISTS. Johnny Cash '18 Greatest Hits' (2026-08-07): embedded and folder passes found nothing, and the album is not in Apple's catalogue at all. There is no image to improve. Upscaling is irrelevant here; only another SOURCE helps.

PROBLEM TWO — ARTWORK EXISTS BUT IS POOR. Embedded art from an older rip at 300x300, or a small cover.jpg beside the files. Here there is a real image and the question is whether it can be made presentable.

--- SOURCES (problem one) ---
Exhaust real originals before reconstructing anything. Apple at full size is the free first step (fArtworkHigherResolutionFetch). Then Cover Art Archive / MusicBrainz, which frequently holds 1000px+ scans Apple does not and has no API key or commercial terms. Discogs has deep compilation coverage but needs OAuth and is rate limited. Last.fm is largely redundant with the above. User-supplied art (fArtworkManagement) is the backstop.

Worth considering as the final fallback: a GENERATED TYPOGRAPHIC COVER from the artist and album name. It is visibly not a photograph of a real sleeve, so it never pretends to be authentic, and it reads far better in a grid than a grey music note. Cheap, offline, and honest.

--- UPSCALING (problem two) ---
ARCHITECTURE — NOT A VETO, A TRADE. CLAUDE.md requires no backend for CORE functionality, and Tom's position is that upscaling album art is not core to a music app. That is the right reading: an opt-in enhancement is not the same as the app needing a server to play music. So on-device is preferred but hosted is permissible if on-device quality proves inadequate — the objections to hosting become ordinary product costs (a service to run and pay for, users' artwork sent to a third party) rather than a breach of principle.

On-device options: a super-resolution model converted to Core ML (Real-ESRGAN and SwinIR both have working ports) running on the Neural Engine. No network, no per-image cost, no privacy question. Costs app bundle size — roughly 5-60MB depending on the model — which is the real trade to evaluate. Core Image and Metal offer only interpolation, which is sharpening rather than reconstruction and not worth shipping.

Server-side options, for completeness: Replicate hosts Real-ESRGAN/SwinIR/GFPGAN behind a simple pay-per-run API; Stability AI has conservative and creative upscale endpoints. Both are straightforward to integrate and both violate the no-backend principle. A self-hosted Real-ESRGAN on the Mac mini is viable for Tom's own library on his LAN, but is not a shippable answer for anyone else — worth knowing as a way to EVALUATE model quality cheaply before committing to a bundled model.

NOT AVAILABLE: Claude cannot do this. The Anthropic API reads images but has no image generation or upscaling endpoint. A ChatGPT result that looked good is evidence the approach works, not that this API can deliver it.

--- THE HAZARD, specific to album art ---
Generative upscalers invent detail, and on a record sleeve the detail is usually the band name. A sharpened 300px cover will contain plausible, confidently wrong letterforms. That is a worse outcome than a soft image, because it looks correct. Treat upscaling as cosmetic smoothing for art that exists nowhere better — never as repair, and never applied silently to something the user might reasonably believe is the real sleeve. Keeping the original alongside the enhanced version, and making the enhancement reversible, is the minimum.

UPSCALING MUST APPLY TO MANUALLY-ADDED ART, NOT ONLY TO SCANNED ART. Confirmed by the Johnny Cash case on 2026-08-07: the album folder contains no image at all — correctly, the scanner found nothing — but Tom has a 14KB scan of the sleeve from elsewhere. Whether a poor image arrives from an old rip, from a folder, or because the user found one on the internet and added it by hand, the end state is identical: a very low resolution cover sitting in the library. If enhancement only ran inside the scan passes, art added through fArtworkManagement would never benefit — which is exactly the art most likely to need it, since a user only goes hunting when the automated passes have already failed. Enhancement belongs on the album, triggerable after the fact, not as a step inside a scan.

SEQUENCING: sources first, upscaling last. Every real original found is one image that never needs reconstructing.

features.name: The share row says 'Never scanned' while its scan is running
features.desc:
During an active scan the ScanStatusPanel says 'Scanning library…' while the share row directly beneath it says 'Never scanned'. Two surfaces on the same screen contradicting each other, observed 2026-08-08 immediately after fAutoScanOnShareAdd landed.

The row derives its subtitle from lastScanned, which is null until a scan finishes, so a first scan reads as though nothing has ever happened. The row already understands some scan states — 'Retrying skipped tracks…' is handled — so 'scanning' simply is not among them.

WHY THIS ONLY MATTERS NOW. Before auto-scan, a scan could only begin after tapping through a confirmation, so the user was already looking at the panel when it started and the row was never the thing they read. Scans now start on their own: you add a share, put the phone down, come back, and the ROW is what you see first. A row that says 'Never scanned' about a scan in progress is the same class of wrongness as a zone card showing a station that stopped hours ago.

Fix is small — teach the row the 'scanning' state alongside 'retrying'. Worth pairing with bTrackCountIgnoresRetryResolved, since both are the row telling the truth about work it did not watch.

features.name: Let the user stop a running scan, and start it again on purpose
features.desc:
Two different things have both been called 'resume' and only one exists.

WHAT EXISTS is CRASH RECOVERY. A scan that dies — killed app, wedged pipeline — leaves the source in 'scanning', and the next foreground raises Scan Incomplete offering Resume / Start Over / Cancel, with Resume continuing from the ledger. Proven through a real crash on 2026-08-06.

WHAT DOES NOT EXIST is a STOP CONTROL. scanTask?.cancel() is reachable only from wedged-pipeline recovery and from restarting a scan on the same source. A user cannot halt a running scan except by force-quitting the app. The ledger makes that safe, but it is not a feature.

WHY IT MATTERS MORE SINCE 2026-08-08: fAutoScanOnShareAdd means scans now start WITHOUT being asked for. Adding a share at 9pm begins a scan whose only escape is killing the app. Tolerable on a 95-file test share; not on Tom's 11,670-file library.

A STOP BUTTON IS THE SMALL VERSION and probably enough on its own: the cancel machinery exists, and a stopped scan lands in exactly the state the Scan Incomplete dialog already handles, so resume comes free. Two caveats measured 2026-08-08: that dialog appears on the next FOREGROUND rather than immediately, so stopping gives no prompt until you leave and return; and its wording ('did not complete') is written for a crash and reads oddly for a deliberate stop.

Deliberate pause with a visible resume, placed properly, belongs with the UI redesign.

features.name: Timestamp the scan, artwork, retry and ledger lines in the status panel
features.desc:
ScanStatusPanel shows the last several pipeline messages with no times, so you cannot tell when any of them happened. A few lines carry a time by accident because it is baked into their text ('START full scan — AV-Server at 21:45:40'); the rest — filter results, ledger plans, artwork passes, retry outcomes — carry none.

THE QUESTION A TIMESTAMP ANSWERS is not 'when did this run' but 'is this stuck'. A panel showing nine lines tells you nothing about whether the last one landed two seconds ago or forty minutes ago, and those are entirely different situations. Without a time the panel cannot distinguish working from wedged.

WHY IT MATTERS MORE SINCE fAutoScanOnShareAdd, 2026-08-08: scans now start without being asked for, so the user ARRIVES at the panel mid-scan rather than watching it from the beginning. Before, you tapped through a confirmation and saw the lines appear in sequence, which gave you the timing for free. Now you come back to a static list.

RELATIVE TIMES ARE THE RIGHT FORM. '40m ago' on the last line says wedged in a way '21:45:40' does not — the reader should not have to subtract. Absolute time can sit alongside for the scan report, where the record matters more than the diagnosis.

NEARLY FREE, because the app already tracks this: ScanCoordinator keeps lastPipelineProgress and compares it against pipelineStallThreshold to detect a wedged pipeline and recover it. The moment of last progress is already known and acted upon — it simply is not shown. The change is to carry a Date alongside each message (statusMessages is currently [String]) and let the view format it, rather than prefixing text at append time and baking the format into the data.

Pairs with bShareRowReadsNeverScannedWhileScanning: both are the scan telling the user less than it knows.

features.name: The screen stops locking — auto-lock is suppressed on every foreground and latches off
features.desc:
Reported 2026-08-08: 'most times the app does not go to lock screen. it stays active all the time' with the device set to lock after 30 seconds.

TWO FAULTS THAT COMPOUND.

ONE — IT IS A ONE-WAY LATCH. UIApplication.isIdleTimerDisabled is set true at the top of runScan (ScanCoordinator ~491). The reset that matters sits at the very END of a Task.detached, after the artwork passes AND after `await ScanRetryScheduler.shared.start(...)`, behind a `guard let self else { return }`. So it is not cleared when the scan finishes — it is cleared when the whole asynchronous chain finishes. Any cancellation, hang, throw or early return between those two points leaves auto-lock disabled, and NOTHING ELSE ever sets it false, so the phone stays awake until the app is killed. One miss is permanent. The other two resets do not save it: one fires only in the catch, the other only in wedged-pipeline recovery.

TWO — IT IS SET CONSTANTLY. runScan executes on EVERY foreground, because every foreground runs a change check. On Tom's 11,670-file library that pipeline measures ~16.9s (bChangeCheckRunsFullPipelineOnNoChange), so auto-lock is suppressed for roughly seventeen seconds every time the app is opened, by design. Frequent exposure plus a one-way failure is why the symptom is 'most times' rather than 'occasionally'.

FIX — DERIVE IT, DO NOT TOGGLE IT. The flag should follow from state: when activeScanSourceId becomes nil, auto-lock returns. That makes it a consequence rather than a pair of statements that must stay balanced across an async boundary. Add a safety net on entering the foreground — clear it before anything sets it — so even a future bug cannot survive an app switch.

SAME SHAPE AS bZoneOrderLostByTopologyMerge: an invariant maintained by matching statements at a distance, which fails the moment one path skips one. Pair with bChangeCheckRunsFullPipelineOnNoChange — one removes the exposure, the other removes the latch.

features.name: Change-check walk should checkpoint and resume, never restart from the top
features.desc:
The automatic change check walks the entire share tree on every foreground and keeps no record of how far it got. If the app is terminated mid-walk, the next launch starts again from the top. On a large library with short sessions this can livelock: every foreground pays for a walk that never finishes, so changes are never detected and the library silently stops updating.

REQUIREMENT. The walk must checkpoint its position and resume from it, so that progress accumulates across foregrounds and a complete pass is guaranteed regardless of how briefly the app is open on any one occasion.

REQUIREMENT. Resumption is automatic and silent. The change check is a background process the user did not initiate, so it must never present a dialog, a confirmation, or a resume prompt under any circumstance.

SCOPE NOTE — suspension versus termination. Backgrounding the app suspends the walk and it resumes where it froze, so ordinary app switching already loses nothing. This work addresses termination under memory pressure, which is the case that restarts from zero.

SIZING. One measurement exists: approximately 17 seconds total on an 11,670-file library, the majority of which is the walk. Linear extrapolation suggests roughly 25 seconds at 20k files and 50 seconds at 40k, but this is derived from a single data point. Cost is one SMB directory listing per folder, so folder count is the driver rather than file count. Measure across real library sizes before designing to any figure.

IMPLEMENTATION DIRECTION. The walk already visits folders sequentially and compares each against a stored fingerprint. Persisting folder-level progress mirrors what the scan ledger already does for per-file outcomes. An open decision remains: how stale a partial walk may become before it should be discarded and restarted.

RELATED. The silent-resumption requirement was partially satisfied on 2026-08-08 — a killed automatic check that had planned no work now resets without raising a scan-interrupted dialog. Checkpointing remains outstanding.

features.name: Auto-lock stays suppressed if a user-initiated scan's pipeline wedges
features.desc:
Auto-lock is derived from activeScanSourceId as of 2026-08-08, so the timer is correct whenever that state is correct. That state is not always correct: activeScanSourceId is cleared at the end of a detached pipeline, and a pipeline that hangs or is cancelled mid-flight leaves it set. The screen then stays awake until the app is killed.

SCOPE. Automatic change checks are unaffected — they no longer engage the idle timer at all — so exposure is limited to scans the user starts whose pipeline subsequently wedges. This is a narrower version of bAutoLockNeverRestored, which was closed the same day: deriving the flag removed the four-statements-at-a-distance failure, but it cannot make the underlying state reliable.

EXISTING MACHINERY. lastPipelineProgress already serves as a stall heartbeat, and the wedge-recovery branch in checkForChanges already clears activeScanSourceId — but only on the next foreground, which requires the user to return to the app. A screen that will not lock is precisely the situation where they may not.

FIX DIRECTION. Clear activeScanSourceId on a progress timeout rather than waiting for a foreground to notice.

features.name: On-disk tag edits not detected by folder change detection
features.desc:
FolderStat change detection compares fileCount and totalBytes per folder. External taggers such as dbPoweramp, Picard, Yate and Mp3tag write tag changes into the FLAC PADDING block reserved for that purpose, so neither file count nor total byte size changes and the folder is never flagged for rescan. Sorriva shows stale metadata indefinitely after a user retags their library. Requires a stronger change signal, such as per-file modified timestamp in FolderStat, or a user-triggered rescan that bypasses FolderStat entirely.

PARTIALLY ADDRESSED 2026-07-30: fUnifiedScanWalkThenFilter added newest-mtime to the folder fingerprint, which is what allows a tag-only edit to be detected -- taggers write into the FLAC PADDING block, so file count and total bytes are unchanged but mtime is not. NOT YET VERIFIED: the matching direction is proven (an unchanged folder correctly skips), but no test has confirmed that a changed mtime with identical size triggers a rescan, because no way to edit a file was available during testing. This matters more than before -- manual rescan used to re-read every header, which was the de facto workaround for retagging, and under the unified model that workaround is gone. Test: `touch` a file over SMB without changing content, then rescan and confirm that folder is scanned.

VERIFIED AND CLOSED 2026-07-31 with a real Mp3tag edit, through BOTH paths. Manual scan: 'filter — skipping 132 file(s) in 12 unchanged folder(s); 0 new, 1 changed' and the folder rescanned. Foreground change check: same result with no user action. Artwork markers reset for that one folder only, and the album's artwork correctly re-evaluated. mtime is what makes this detectable — the tag write left file count and total bytes unchanged, exactly as predicted.

Correct for single-artist albums, arbitrary for compilations — a VA compilation spanning multiple genres takes the genre of track 1 for the entire album. Per-track genre is stored correctly on Track and is unaffected; only the album-level rollup is wrong. Interim fix is to take the most common genre across the album's tracks during scan finalize. Expected to be resolved properly by external metadata enrichment. RESOLVED 2026-07-26, differently than originally scoped: rather than "most common genre wins" (still an arbitrary single answer for a genuinely mixed-genre compilation), built a proper v14 album_genres many-to-many table — mirrors station_genres' structural pattern (composite PK, cascade FK) but stores raw freeform genre strings rather than joining to a curated taxonomy, since local tag genres aren't drawn from a fixed list. Album.genre (single-value) is untouched — confirmed nothing in the UI reads it today, so this is purely additive. Populated from the distinct genres actually present across an album's tracks at scan finalize; rescans clear-then-rewrite so retagging doesn't accumulate stale entries. 3 new tests (AlbumGenreTests.swift), all passing.

features.name: Online artwork accepted the first search result without checking who it was by
features.desc:
CORRECTED 2026-07-27: original diagnosis ("query sends only album title, not artist name") is stale and does not match the current code — ArtworkCache.searchURL(artist:album:) has always built the query as "\(artist) \(cleanAlbum)", including both. Re-confirmed affected via a second real case tonight: Johnny Cash '18 Greatest Hits' received Al Green's artwork despite the artist name being present in the query. The real problem is broader than a missing query term — iTunes Search API's own relevance ranking plus ArtworkCache.parseArtworkURL's unconditional acceptance of results.first (zero verification the returned result is even plausibly related) is unreliable for generic/common titles ("Greatest Hits", "Various Artists" compilations) regardless of what's in the query. KEPT OPEN deliberately — worth a real discussion and some query-tuning experiments (e.g. quoting/formatting changes, or checking the response's own artistName/collectionName fields against the query before accepting a match) before deciding whether better query construction alone can meaningfully improve this, versus needing the human-in-the-loop approach in fArtworkManualSearchUtility instead. IMMEDIATE MITIGATION 2026-07-27: online fetch (ArtworkCache.fetchArtwork) reverted to only running for albums with zero existing art (matches original, pre-2026-07-27-redesign behavior) — a wrong match can no longer overwrite correct existing artwork, only fill a genuine gap. See bArtworkSelectionNotBestWins for what changed and why.

FIXED 2026-08-07. Reproduced live first: the old query for 'Johnny Cash 18 Greatest Hits' returned CREED's Greatest Hits that morning, having returned Al Green's in July. Not a near-miss — a different artist, accepted because parseArtworkURL took results.first and never looked at the artistName beside it.

Fixed structurally rather than by tuning the query. New ArtworkLookup.swift resolves the ARTIST first (entity=musicArtist), then searches only that artist's catalogue (lookup?id=&entity=album), so a wrong-artist match stops being expressible instead of being filtered out afterwards. artistId is cached per artist, which makes this CHEAPER than the old single-call version on any library with several albums per artist. Falls back to the old text search with artist verification when an artist is not in iTunes, and declines outright for compilation placeholders, which have no artist to constrain by.

Acceptance threshold 0.62, set from measurement: across eight real albums against the live API, every correct match scored 0.75+ and every wrong one 0.57 or less. Johnny Cash '18 Greatest Hits' is not in Apple's catalogue at all, so it now gets NO artwork rather than wrong artwork — the correct outcome, and the residue that fArtworkManualSearchUtility exists to handle.

12 unit tests (ArtworkLookupTests). They caught a real defect before it shipped: containment was scored symmetrically, so 'Greatest' sitting inside '18 Greatest Hits' scored 0.75 and an album literally titled Greatest would have been auto-accepted. Containment is now asymmetric — a candidate CONTAINING the whole wanted title scores high, a candidate that is merely a FRAGMENT of it falls through to token overlap.

RESIZED XS->M at close. The XS was set against the original diagnosis ("query omits artist name"), which the code never actually did — so the estimate was priced for a one-line change to a problem that did not exist. The real fix was a new module, a schema migration, twelve unit tests and calibration against the live API. Recording the honest number rather than the one that was guessed before the problem was understood.

features.name: Import a Spotify library into Sorriva — migration, not integration
features.desc:
Import a user's existing Spotify library into Sorriva as LIBRARY INTENT, without Sorriva ever streaming Spotify audio or holding a live Spotify integration. Sorriva ingests the library, resolves each recording against the sources it actually supports, and builds its own library from the matches.

THE PRINCIPLE, and it is the whole point: SPOTIFY IS AN IMPORT NAMESPACE, NOT A PROVIDER. Where a user's library CAME FROM is separated from where Sorriva OBTAINS the audio. Spotify ids are kept as provenance and matching keys, never as playback identifiers.

WHY IT MATTERS. Spotify's Web API is gated behind a user threshold no personal project can meet — this was established on 2026-08-11 and closed the door on Spotify as a real source. But a user with 10,000 saved tracks does not need Spotify playback for those 10,000 tracks to become useful; Sorriva only needs to know which recordings the user considers theirs. It removes the largest switching barrier a streaming user has, which is rebuilding years of saved music by hand.

GATED ON HAVING SOMEWHERE TO RESOLVE TO. Tom's condition, 2026-08-16: this comes into play once at least one track-level streaming service is integrated. `requires` names fMusicKitAdapter because it is the only such entry on the roadmap; Qobuz or TIDAL would satisfy the gate equally. Without one, an import can only resolve against the NAS — see the phasing below, which is the honest way to get value before that lands.

INPUT — FILES, NOT AN API.
- PREFERRED: the user's own Spotify account-data export (ZIP/JSON), requested from Spotify directly. No third party in the chain.
- ALSO: structured exports from Soundiiz, TuneMyMusic and similar (CSV/JSON/TXT), for users who do not want to wait for Spotify's export process.
- The architecture must NOT depend on a direct Spotify API path. If policy ever permits one it is an additional input, never the foundation.

ISRC IS PROBABLY NOT AVAILABLE, AND THE SOURCE DOCUMENT ASSUMES IT IS. ISRC is a Web API field; the personal data export carries roughly track name, artist, album and URI. VERIFY AGAINST A REAL EXPORT BEFORE DESIGNING THE MATCHER — if ISRC is absent, the preferred exact-match tier does not exist and matching begins at artist + title + album + duration, which is materially weaker. Related: the '99.2% match rate' figure in the source document is invented and nothing supports it. Do not carry expectations from it into the UI copy.

MATCHING, best tier first: ISRC exact; album identifier/UPC; artist + normalised title + album; artist + normalised title + duration; fuzzy metadata last. Normalisation must absorb remaster and anniversary and deluxe suffixes, explicit/clean variants, featured-artist formatting, parenthetical version text, punctuation, unicode and case. Every match carries a confidence — EXACT / HIGH / MEDIUM / LOW — and LOW requires confirmation rather than being silently accepted.

ONE RECORDING, MANY SOURCES. A track available locally AND on a streaming provider is ONE library item with several source mappings, never duplicate rows; playback then follows Sorriva's existing source priority. NOTE THIS IS REAL SCHEMA WORK Sorriva has not done — today there are local tracks and service stations, with no canonical recording that several providers can satisfy. It overlaps fPlaybackConductor and fMusicKitAdapter and should be designed with them, not separately.

PLAYLISTS keep their original order. Unmatched tracks REMAIN VISIBLE as unresolved placeholders rather than silently vanishing, so the user can fix them later.

RE-IMPORT IS RECONCILIATION, NOT SYNC. Importing again reports what changed — new tracks, new and changed playlists, and items no longer saved on Spotify. Sorriva MUST NOT delete anything from its own library because Spotify no longer lists it; removal is the user's decision. Import must be idempotent: the same file twice creates no duplicates. Provenance kept per item (importSource, spotifyTrackId, importDate).

PHASING, so this is not all-or-nothing:
1. LOCAL ONLY — 'which of my saved Spotify tracks do I already own?' Parse the export, normalise, match against the NAS library. Needs no streaming provider, no ISRC and no canonical-source model, and is useful to Tom immediately. This is the front half of the full pipeline, not throwaway.
2. PROVIDER RESOLUTION — once a track-level service exists, resolve the misses against it and build the multi-source canonical records.

LONGER TERM the same importer shape serves Apple Music, TIDAL, Qobuz, Roon, Plex, CSV, M3U and MusicBrainz exports — a generic import framework with Spotify as the first importer. Build it as one importer with a normalised intermediate record; do not build the framework speculatively before the second importer exists.

ORIGIN: drafted by Tom from a ChatGPT-generated document, 2026-08-16. The strategic framing is his and is sound; the caveats above (ISRC availability, the invented match rate, the assumed integrations, the missing canonical model) are corrections made when it was assessed against the actual codebase.

===================== STATUS, 2026-08-18 =====================

SLICE A IS BUILT AND PROVEN. It is a proof that the plumbing works, NOT the feature. Search Apple's catalogue from Discover, open an album, play it on a zone, and the zone reports the right track, artist, album, artwork and duration. Apple Music shows as Connected in Services when the household's Sonos reports service 204.

WHAT SLICE A DELIBERATELY DOES NOT DO, and what the rest of this entry is:
  - NOTHING PERSISTS. There are no Apple Music rows anywhere. Close the app and there is no record that an album was ever found. No save, no favorite, no recently-played.
  - IT IS NOT IN THE LIBRARY. Albums and Artists show local FLAC only. A saved Apple album must land in the same Albums view as a NAS album -- mixed sources for the same media type is a foundation requirement, and none of it is wired.
  - NO TRACK-LEVEL PLAY. The address plumbing exists and is tested (playAppleMusicTracks, the no-<res> DIDL) but no UI calls it. A whole album plays; nothing smaller does.
  - NO PLAYLISTS. Neither Apple's nor the user's own. A playlist mixing a FLAC track with an Apple track is the point of track-level enqueue, and it is unbuilt.
  - NO BROWSE. A search box only. No artist page, no more-by-this-artist, no genre or new-releases.

===================== THE ARCHITECTURE =====================

THE ORIGINAL AIRPLAY PREMISE WAS WRONG -- measured 2026-08-18. Apple Music does not have to be decoded on the phone and AirPlayed. Sonos fetches it directly and Sorriva can CONSTRUCT the addresses:

  song      x-sonos-http:song%3a<catalogueId>.mp4?sid=204&flags=8232&sn=5
  container x-rincon-cpcontainer:00040000album%3a<collectionId>?sid=204&flags=0&sn=5

Both were built from parts and played on speakers that had never been given them. Full shapes, the cdudn token, the DIDL rules and the command sequence are in sonos-playback-contract.md 13.

SO THE ARCHITECTURE INVERTS. Apple's endpoints supply IDENTIFIERS AND METADATA; SONOS does the playing. The phone stays out of the audio path -- the property local FLAC has and every streaming source has lacked. ApplicationMusicPlayer and AirPlay become the fallback for endpoints that are not Sonos, not the primary path.

INDIVIDUAL SONGS ARE ADDRESSABLE, which is worth more than container playback: a queue can mix local FLAC and Apple Music track by track. That is fPlaybackConductor's premise and it has never had a route to it until now.

TWO IDENTIFIER SPACES must both be handled -- a global catalogue id (numeric) and a per-account library id (l./i. prefixed) for anything the user has added.

===================== THREE PARTS, INDEPENDENT =====================

Treating them as one thing is what made this entry describe an AirPlay design for a year.

  1. FINDING MUSIC -- Apple's public catalogue endpoints. No account, no key, no entitlement. PROVEN.
  2. PLAYING MUSIC -- Sonos, handed an address Sorriva builds. PROVEN.
  3. PERSONAL DATA -- MusicKit, for the user's own library and playlists. Needs entitlement + auth. NOT STARTED.

Parts 1 and 2 together are a complete, useful product. Part 3 is an upgrade, not a prerequisite.

WHY MUSICKIT IS STILL NEEDED even for an empty library: the public search is RELEVANCE, not structure. "Pat Metheny" returned a Jaco Pastorius record, a Kronos Quartet album and an unrelated Japanese guitar record, plus the same album twice under two ids. There is no "this artist's albums" call. MusicKit has real artist relationships and returns a discography. So MusicKit is required for CORRECT BROWSING, independently of whether the user has anything saved.

===================== MEASURED FACTS =====================

WHAT THE PUBLIC ENDPOINTS GIVE:
  search   artists, albums, songs, each with a catalogue id
  lookup   an album's full track list -- track and disc numbers, durations, isStreamable
  album    genre, release date, track count, label copyright, artwork
  artwork  one url whose path carries the size: 100/600/1000/3000 all verified to fetch
Limits: 200 results per search with NO paging; roughly 20 requests a minute.

THE CATALOGUE IS NOT THE SERVICE. The iTunes Store catalogue and Apple Music's catalogue disagree, and not only at the margins. One Metheny album reported 9 tracks and returned 8. Vanessa Daou's "Slow to Burn" reported 11 tracks and returned NONE, while Sonos resolved all 11 through the service. CONSEQUENCE: an album must remain playable when its track list is empty, and a missing track list must never disable Play. isStreamable exists; do not trust it blindly.

THE <res> RULE, and it looks backwards. Supplying a <res> element in the DIDL makes Sonos take our word for the resource: it stores application/octet-stream and reports TrackDuration 0:00:00 forever. OMIT IT, give the item its object id and the household token, and Sonos resolves the track through the service, returning application/x-mpegURL and the real length. This cost most of a session because a first failed attempt omitted <res> AND used id="-1" AND had no token; "res is required" was recorded as the lesson and was the wrong variable.

THE TOKEN COMES FROM A SONOS FAVORITE, not from Sorriva's database. Every favorite of a service embeds the same cdudn, so ONE saved Apple Music favorite is enough, and Apple Music has no rows in Sorriva's stations table to read. Reading locally found nothing even when the household plainly had the credential -- a real bug on 2026-08-18. SETTLED: the token is REQUIRED for containers and for metadata-bearing tracks, and NOT required for a bare-URI track play.

SA_RINCON<n> = sid * 256 + 7, verified across every service in the household (iHeart 6 -> 1543, Spotify 12 -> 3079, SiriusXM 37 -> 9479, Sonos Radio 303 -> 77575, Apple 204 -> 52231). Only the account half ever needs discovering.

CONSTRAINTS ON PLAYBACK:
  1. The household's Sonos needs Apple Music added with an ACTIVE SUBSCRIPTION. Done once in the Sonos app; Sorriva cannot create that linkage. Bluesound will be the same shape.
  2. Content must be in the streaming catalogue, not purchase-only.
  3. Catalogue ids are storefront-specific. UNTESTED against a non-US account.
  4. NOTHING requires content to be in the user's library. This is the whole difference from Spotify, where favorites were the only reachable content. One Sonos favorite is needed for the token, not for the content.

===================== BUILD ORDER =====================

  A. DONE -- search the catalogue, open an album, play it on a zone.

  B. SAVE. Apple albums held LOCALLY in Sorriva as rows of catalogue ids. Nothing is written to Apple Music; the Music app is never opened. FIRST, because nothing else can exist until an Apple album can be stored.

  C. LIBRARY INTEGRATION. Saved Apple albums appear in Albums and Artists alongside NAS albums, with the source visible so available actions can differ by source and by what is reachable (NAS, internet, Sonos). Service albums currently ride under Radio because a Spotify album had no track listing to justify the mixed-source model (fStationMediaType). An Apple album has a full track list, release date, label and cover art, so the model now has a real reason to exist and should be built ONCE, for local and streaming albums together.

  D. TRACK-LEVEL PLAY. UI for playing and enqueuing single tracks. The addresses and DIDL already exist and are tested; this is the surface, not the plumbing.

  E. PLAYLISTS. Sorriva-owned playlists that can hold a local FLAC track and an Apple Music track in the same list -- which Apple's own library cannot do. Depends on D.

  F. BROWSE. Artist pages, more-by-this-artist, genre, new releases. Wants MusicKit for artist-correct structure, so this is where part 3 enters.

  G. OPTIONAL -- mirror Sorriva playlists INTO Apple Music for portability. Sync Library uploads the user's own NAS collection to the cloud as AAC 256, so a mixed playlist CAN mirror in full, at lossy quality, while the at-home copy still plays the original FLAC.

===================== OPEN, NOT TO BE ASSUMED =====================

  - Whether MusicKit can play ALREADY-DOWNLOADED Apple Music with no connection. An on-device test. Expectation: playback works, but the download can only be started in the Music app, which makes it a poor experience regardless.
  - Offline for the user's OWN library is a different and solvable thing: cache FLAC to the phone from the NAS. That means Sorriva grows a local player for the first time, so it is real work, not a setting.
  - Non-US storefront behaviour.
  - This drives a service integration through an interface Sonos publishes for its own app. Worth a clear-eyed look before it SHIPS, which is not the same as before it is investigated.

===================== 2026-08-19 — DESIGN NOW LIVES ELSEWHERE =====================

Slices B-E of the build order below are superseded in DETAIL by engineering/apple-music-library-model.md, agreed with Tom 2026-08-19. That document is the authority for the data model, the migration, feature parity with local playback, and the sequencing. This entry remains the parent and its A-G order still holds.

WHAT CHANGED. The model is normalized rather than flat: common album/track/playlist tables joined to a source-specific table per source, foreign key in the child. Tracked as fSourceNormalizedSchema, which is the prerequisite for B onward. Discover becoming a hub is split out as fDiscoverHub and goes FIRST because it decides nothing about data. Availability and quality display, both surfaced by this work, are fAvailabilityModel and fTrackQualityDisplay, the latter blocked by bAudioQualityNeverCaptured.

SEARCH QUALITY — RECHECK BEFORE ACTING. The measured note above records 'Pat Metheny' returning a Jaco Pastorius record and a Kronos Quartet album. Re-run 2026-08-19 it returned five genuine Metheny albums. The premise may have moved.

===================== 2026-08-20 — MEASURED CORRECTIONS =====================

THREE CLAIMS ABOVE ARE NOW KNOWN TO BE WRONG. They are left in place rather than edited out, because each one was cited as a REASON elsewhere and the correction matters more than the tidiness.

1. "There is no 'this artist's albums' call" — WRONG. Both the public lookup endpoint and MusicKit return a proper discography with artwork. MusicKit goes much further: albums, singles, compilationAlbums, liveAlbums, appearsOnAlbums, topSongs, playlists, similarArtists, latestRelease and station are all separate relationships, read out of the MusicKit SDK interface rather than remembered. The whole artist page is built on them. This claim was the stated reason browse "wants MusicKit" — the conclusion held, the reason did not.

2. "'Pat Metheny' returns a Jaco Pastorius record and a Kronos Quartet album" — NO LONGER REPRODUCES. Re-run 2026-08-20: 25 results, all genuinely Metheny, zero duplicate title+artist pairs. 3. "Curated playlists may not need MusicKit" (apple-music-library-model.md 6) — THEY DO. Separately, the extra playlists Apple Music shows for an artist search are USER-GENERATED and catalogue search does not expose them, so our playlist counts will stay lower than the Apple Music app's.

PART 3 IS NO LONGER 'NOT STARTED'. MusicKit is integrated and is now the ONLY catalogue source; the public iTunes path is superseded. Catalogue search needs no subscription and no signed-in Apple ID, and the permission prompt is shown once and remembered. Slices D (track-level play surface), F (browse) and the Apple half of E landed with fDiscoverHub.
