features.name: Sonos GENA event subscriptions - push transport state instead of polling
features.desc:
Replace poll-based transport/zone state with Sonos GENA (UPnP General Event Notification Architecture) event subscriptions. The app SUBSCRIBEs to each speaker's AVTransport and RenderingControl services; Sonos then pushes an HTTP NOTIFY to an in-app callback (via the existing in-app HTTP server, fLocalHTTPServer) the instant transport, track, or volume changes, instead of Sorriva polling every 2-5s. Benefits: near-instant updates, no poll-interval latency, far less network chatter, and it dissolves the external-change staleness window that the PlaybackStore rearchitecture otherwise mitigates with hold-last-good. Requires subscription lifecycle management: renew before timeout, re-subscribe on network change, unsubscribe on teardown. Strategic note: had GENA been known at design time, the transport layer would have been built on it from the start. Sequenced as a future tightening AFTER the PlaybackStore authoritative-declaration rearchitecture is stable and ZoneDiscoveryService is decomposed, at which point poll-to-push can be swapped behind the same transport interface without changing anything above it.

SECOND OPTION, ADDED 2026-08-08 — the Sonos local control API. Reachable on port 1443 of any player; returns ERROR_API_KEY_VALIDATION_FAILED without credentials, so it needs a registered integration. It offers a real subscription model and a richer playback state than UPnP exposes. It is OAuth, so a Sonos account login inside Sorriva — but an initial reading that this therefore requires a backend was WRONG: native apps use PKCE with a custom-scheme redirect the app handles itself, the same shape Tidal and others will need anyway, so the no-backend property survives. Real costs are a second protocol alongside UPnP and a dependency on Sonos keeping the programme open to non-commercial developers (unconfirmed; the partner docs describe Company accounts and imply but do not state an individual path).

SO THIS ITEM IS NOW A CHOICE, NOT A PLAN: GENA (no credentials, uses the in-app HTTP server, well-understood) versus the control API (richer state, needs a key and an account login). Evaluate them together — they answer the same question and should not be pursued in parallel.

EVIDENCE THAT THE 'EXTERNAL CHANGES' ARGUMENT IS THE STRONG ONE: bGroupChangesMadeOutsideSorrivaAreNeverSeen, found 2026-08-08. A grouping change made from the Sonos app, a voice command or TV autoplay is invisible to Sorriva until relaunch. That is precisely the staleness window this entry describes, and it is now a demonstrated defect rather than a theoretical one. Note it also has a cheap poll-side fix, which should land first — push is the right long-term answer, not the urgent one.

NOT A REASON TO DO THIS: distinguishing a live TV from a selected input. That question prompted the 2026-08-08 look and turned out to be answerable over plain UPnP via ZoneGroupTopology's IdleState — see sonos-playback-contract.md 6a.

THE ARGUMENT CHANGED 2026-08-16: THIS IS NOW THE IDENTITY MECHANISM, NOT A LATENCY OPTIMISATION. Measured on Patio (192.168.1.194) while a Spotify playlist played. Two AVTransport state variables, r:EnqueuedTransportURI and r:EnqueuedTransportURIMetaData, carry the URI ORIGINALLY handed to the speaker and the metadata that came with it:

  r:EnqueuedTransportURI
    x-rincon-cpcontainer:1006206cspotify%3Aplaylist%3A37i9dQZF1DX3jWba5xiDhV?sid=12&flags=8300&sn=2
  r:EnqueuedTransportURIMetaData
    <dc:title>Italo Disco</dc:title>
    <upnp:class>object.container.playlistContainer</upnp:class>

THEY HAVE NO GETTER. Verified against the speaker's own AVTransport1.xml: 42 actions, none of which returns them; they appear only in the LastChange event. GetMediaInfo returns CurrentURI=x-rincon-queue:…#0 with CurrentURIMetaData EMPTY, so polling cannot reach this by any route. Reading it required a GENA SUBSCRIBE. Tom predicted it from first principles — the Sonos app displays the playlist name for content IT did not start, so the name has to live on the speaker — and an earlier conclusion here that 'the speaker will not tell us' was wrong.

WHY THIS MATTERS BEYOND SPOTIFY. The enqueued URI is what was sent to the speaker, which is the FAVORITE we imported. That makes station identity one mechanism instead of a per-service investigation, and every service so far has cost its own: Sonos Radio took a session (bSonosRadioTitleShownAsStation), SiriusXM is still open (fSiriusXMStationIdentity), Spotify was open until this measurement. It also very likely resolves SiriusXM, whose stored x-sonosapi-stream:channel-linear:… and playing x-sonosapi-hls:channel-linear:… have no common key today.

This also TIPS THE CHOICE recorded above. GENA reaches the enqueued URI with no credentials and no account login; whether the local control API exposes an equivalent is unverified, and it costs a registered integration to find out.

WHAT IT DOES NOT REMOVE, so scope is not overstated:
- The per-service adapters. Events carry the SAME DIDL we parse now, so 'which field holds the song' is unchanged — dc:title is the song for Sonos Radio and Spotify and a filename for iHeart. That ambiguity belongs to the service, not the transport.
- The stations table. Curated names and logos stay ours, and a Sorriva-started iHeart stream sends no metadata today, so the speaker would have nothing to echo back.
- Polling. iOS kills the callback listener on background, so a full state read is still needed at launch and on every foreground, plus a fallback when a subscription lapses. The poll's job shrinks to cold-start reconciliation rather than disappearing.

THE REAL COST IS LIFECYCLE, NOT PARSING: an in-app HTTP listener, a subscription per coordinator, renewal before Sonos's timeout, resubscribe on network change and foreground, and correct behaviour when events are missed. How well that survives iOS backgrounding on Tom's system is NOT measured and should not be assumed.

REPRODUCE: the probe used is scratchpad/gena_probe.py — SUBSCRIBE to /MediaRenderer/AVTransport/Event with a CALLBACK on the Mac, read the initial NOTIFY (Sonos sends full state on subscribe), UNSUBSCRIBE. Note the Sonos-namespaced variables are 'r:'-prefixed in LastChange, and the val= attributes are entity-encoded TWICE.

Sorriva treats a valid-looking dc:title as the station name, so for Sonos Radio the track lands in the station slot. Track and artist stay blank because Sonos Radio does not populate r:streamContent the way iHeart and SomaFM do, and that is where those two fields are read from.

This is exactly the ambiguity the per-service adapters in RadioServiceAdapter.swift exist to resolve, and there is no Sonos Radio adapter — Sonos Radio is not a source in Sorriva, so there are no stored stations to reverse-resolve against. Two options: (1) write a Sonos Radio adapter that knows dc:title is the track and maps the fields correctly, or (2) as a general guard, stop trusting dc:title as a station name whenever no adapter claims the URI, and surface it as track instead. Option 2 is the safer default because it also protects against the next unknown service; option 1 gives a correct station name as well. See engineering/radio-service-integration.md.

FIXED 2026-08-13, and the 2026-08-04 root cause above proved correct in full. Two independent defects sat behind one symptom.

FIRST, IDENTITY. Sonos Radio reports a PER-TRACK TrackURI (x-sonos-http:sonos%3a4375c80b..., different every song) and keeps the station only in CurrentURI (x-sonosapi-radio:sonos%3a158291). Station lookups matched the TRACK URI, so they missed on every song forever and the no-blank rule held whatever Sorriva last played — a zone playing Brit Soul went on reporting Cocktail Hour indefinitely. SonosZone now carries currentStationURI from GetMediaInfo and stationIdentityURI is what every lookup matches on. GetMediaInfo is fetched BEFORE GetPositionInfo, because the now-playing parse asks which service is loaded.

SECOND, NOW-PLAYING. There is now a SonosRadioAdapter, and NowPlayingSource makes the field a SERVICE decision rather than a guess: Sonos Radio reads dc:title / dc:creator / upnp:albumArtURI, iHeart and SomaFM keep r:streamContent untouched, and a service no adapter claims keeps the shipped behaviour instead of a new guess. Per-track artwork is a zone field outranking the station logo, and is cleared rather than held when a song ends — a cover outliving its song is worse than none.

MEASURED, NOT ASSUMED: the stored favorite and the live URI differ in the case of the percent-encoded colon AND in flags (28780 vs 0) for the same station, which is why identity is the channel and everything after '?' is discarded. SonosRadioAdapter deliberately does NOT claim SiriusXM, which also emits x-sonosapi-radio: URIs with a channel-xtra payload.

Verified on the Office speaker: Cocktail Hour from Sorriva, Brit Soul from the Sonos app, back and forth, every switch tracked. CONFIRMED ON A LIVE CARD 2026-08-16, which the close note on 08-13 could not claim: Patio playing Brit Soul showed the song, the artist and the per-track cover (Simply Red, 'Fairground'), with the station named correctly above it.

features.name: Soma Radio track info not received — Sonos shows it, Sorriva does not
features.desc: Soma FM stations surface track and artist metadata in the Sonos native app but Sorriva does not display it. Sonos is receiving the metadata via the stream — Sorriva's polling is either not fetching it or not parsing it correctly for radio streams. Investigate GetPositionInfo / GetMediaInfo responses for Soma stations to identify where the track data is present and wire it into the Now Playing display.

features.name: Last zone in Zones view obstructed by mini player
features.desc: The last zone card in the Zones view is partially cut off by the persistent mini player bar in both collapsed and expanded zone card states. The zone list needs sufficient bottom padding or content inset to clear the mini player height so all zone cards are fully visible and tappable.

features.name: Artist and track name on zone card
features.desc: Display current artist and track name on the zone card when local library playback is active. Currently zone cards show this info for radio stations but not for local tracks. Should appear in the same position as station name/track info on radio zone cards.

features.name: Zone discovery restart loop on uncached devices
features.desc: Discovery restart loop on any device with no cached zone topology. NWPathMonitor invokes pathUpdateHandler immediately on start(), not only on change. The monitor was created inside startDiscovery() and cancelled by stopDiscovery(), so the satisfied callback fired handleNetworkRestored() -> stopDiscovery() -> startDiscovery() -> new monitor -> callback. Approximately 400 iterations/sec; 48,374 cycles observed in 122s on first iPad launch. The NetServiceBrowser was destroyed roughly every 2.5ms, well before Bonjour could resolve any service, so zones never populated and the exit condition was never reachable. Fix: network monitor and both NotificationCenter observers moved to init as service-lifetime concerns; stopDiscovery no longer cancels the monitor; transition-into-satisfied detection added so only a real network change triggers rediscovery; 10s restart floor added as a guard against any future repeating caller. Also fixed in the same pass: both observers were re-registered on every startDiscovery() call and never removed, leaking approximately 96,700 live observers over the captured session. Browser and resolve delegate diagnostics converted from print() to sLog() so Bonjour behaviour reaches the debug export.

features.name: Network-scoped zone topology cache
features.desc: Zone topology cache keyed by IPv4 subnet rather than a single flat UserDefaults key, so a device taken to a different Sonos system restores nothing and discovers fresh. New file NetworkIdentity.swift derives the key from getifaddrs as CIDR (e.g. 192.168.1.0/24) with no entitlements and no permission prompts. Subnet keys collide across locations sharing a common private range, so the cached entry also carries the Sonos household ID from GetZoneGroupAttributes; once real topology arrives the live household is compared against the restored one and the entry is discarded and rewritten on mismatch. syncTopologyToDB now returns the live household ID and the cache write moved to after it, so the household is known at write time. The pre-existing network-agnostic key is deleted on sight and never read. Default gateway was evaluated as an additional key component and rejected: within a given subnet the gateway is almost always x.x.x.1, so it adds no entropy in the exact collision case it was intended to resolve, at the cost of a fragile routing-table walk.

features.name: Scope user-owned state to Sonos household
features.desc: Investigate scoping user-owned state to the Sonos household rather than globally, for users with more than one Sonos system (home plus a second property or a work install). Library sources, favorites, presets, and persisted zone state are currently global, so a home NAS share would appear on a system that cannot reach it. The household ID is already persisted in the households table and validated against cached topology, so the join key exists; the open questions are which entities scope per-household and whether a user-facing household name is surfaced in settings. The raw CurrentMuseHouseholdId is opaque and should stay hidden; if anything is surfaced it should be a friendly name read from GetZoneGroupAttributes and renameable by the user. Distinct from fHouseholdProfiles, which is multi-profile support within one account, not multi-system scoping.

features.name: Per-service radio adapters - each provider identifies its own stations
features.desc: Replace the single global URI-matching heuristic with one adapter per streaming service, each of which knows its provider's URI shape exactly: iHeart by station code (zc8681), SomaFM by channel slug (secretagent). RadioServiceRegistry asks the adapters to identify a stream first and falls back to generic normalisation only for URIs no adapter claims. Tom's call, and the right one: a global rule set accumulates an exception per service and every new provider re-breaks the previous ones -- 'instead of trying to make a global rule set against all radio stations we need code for each service so it is handled exactly as it needs to be'. Adding a service is now a new adapter file rather than an edit to shared matching logic. Integration guide, including what each service does and does not report, in engineering/radio-service-integration.md.

features.name: AIFF tracks scanned with no duration, so no total time when playing
features.desc: The AIFF COMM parser read the 80-bit extended sample rate at the wrong offset -- it took offset+14, which is sampleSize, not the start of the rate field. The exponent came out as 16 instead of ~16398, so 2^(16-16446) underflowed to 0.0, and a zero rate made the duration calculation fail silently: the track scanned fine and played fine, it just had no total time. Fixed by reading the exponent at offset+16 and the full 8-byte mantissa at offset+18. Confirmed on device: AIFF files now show total time.

features.name: Local track loads with artwork and metadata but never starts playing
features.desc: A zone whose transport was left in a wedged state accepted SetAVTransportURI and reported the new track -- artwork, title and artist all updated correctly -- but Play did nothing. Fixed by issuing Stop before SetAVTransportURI on both local playback paths, and by adding verifyPlaybackStarted, which reads GetTransportInfo shortly after the Play command and logs whether the zone actually entered PLAYING. Cost three wrong theories before empirical raw-SOAP testing found it (share registration, .local hostname resolution, and DIDL duration metadata were each blamed and each cleared) -- the verification step exists so the next occurrence is visible rather than inferred.

features.name: Two zones on the same station displayed different names
features.desc: Idle and playing zones had SEPARATE station-resolution implementations that disagreed. The idle one trusted Sonos's dc:title ahead of the stations table and returned early when a name was present, so it never did the lookup at all; its fallback also searched iHeart only, so a SomaFM station could not have resolved there in any case. Result: two zones parked on the same SomaFM stream, one showing the curated 'Groove Salad' and the other the raw slug 'groovesalad-128-aac'. Every fix applied to the playing path left the idle path broken. Fixed by deleting the duplicate -- both paths now call one stationDisplay(for:) resolver where the stations table wins and dc:title is only a fallback. Also fixed in the same place: the resolver discarded its own result when a zone had no context yet (the common idle case), and left the previous local album's embedded artwork in place, which the mini player prefers -- so a station could display wearing an album cover.

features.name: One failed station lookup stranded a zone until the app was force-quit
features.desc: Station lookups are cached per zone to stop them re-running on every poll, and a MISS was cached with no expiry. Since the cache is memory-only, a single failure meant the zone showed the raw stream name until the app was relaunched -- which is exactly the 'closed and relaunched and it self-healed' signature. The trigger was a second defect: a transfer briefly groups the destination to the source, during which Sonos reports its URI as x-rincon: (a speaker address, not a stream). That was being treated as a radio stream and sent to the station lookup, manufacturing a miss. Fixed both: x-rincon: is excluded from the radio-stream test alongside queue and local URIs, and a cached miss now expires after 30s. The expiry is the more valuable half -- the grouping hole is closed, but the pattern of one bad lookup poisoning a zone would have resurfaced with the next unfamiliar URI shape, looking like a different bug each time.

features.name: Radio zone stuck on the track that was playing when the station started
features.desc:
A playing radio zone keeps showing the track and artist that were current at the moment the station was declared, forever. Station name and artwork stay correct. Observed live 2026-08-04: Master Bedroom on iHeart Lost 80s, Sonos reporting Eurythmics and then Prince ~80s later, while the app displayed Chaka Khan -- a song that had played several tracks earlier.

ROOT CAUSE: the reducer's first precedence branch in PlaybackStore.resolveContent -- 'Sonos confirms what we declared, therefore authoritative; polling cannot override'. That is sound for a local file, whose URI changes with every track, so one URI really does mean one piece of content. It is false for a stream: the URI is the STATION (.../zc7934/hls.m3u8) and never changes while the songs do. So the branch matches on every poll forever and returns the snapshot frozen at declare time. Polling reports the correct track continuously and is discarded BY DESIGN.

FIX (BUILT 2026-08-04, compiles clean; left open pending field verification -- Tom is running it for several days to see whether it manifests again): branch the confirmed-URI case on content kind. A local declaration returns unchanged -- the app owns all of it because Sonos has neither the track nor the art. A stream declaration returns its station identity with the LIVE track and artist layered on, since Sonos reports those correctly via r:streamContent and the app cannot know them. Hold the previous track rather than blanking if Sonos reports empty between songs. Confined to resolveContent; the URI check still gates the branch, so a declaration still cannot display a station the zone is not playing.

WIDER POINT, worth keeping: declarations exist to cover the 1-2s gap between the app issuing a command and Sonos confirming it. They were then given permanent authority over content, which is a far bigger claim than that problem needs -- the exception became the rule, and every 'what's playing' ghost is a case where the app's copy went stale and that rule blocked reality from correcting it. Note this is NOT fixed by moving to GENA event subscriptions: push changes how the app learns of a change, not what it does with it, so the same rule would freeze content just as hard. See HANDOFF-playbackstore-design.md sections 3.1 and 12.1. BLOCKS phases C/D/E.

CLOSED 2026-08-08 on Tom's field observation — not seen since everything was consolidated into PlaybackStore. Closing on absence alone would be weak, so what supports it: the fix was confirmedContent, which drew the compositional boundary explicitly — the app owns station identity (name and logo), Sonos owns what is playing right now via r:streamContent. A declaration bound to a station URI no longer pins the track that happened to be playing when the station started, because the URI never changes while the songs do. It is also guarded by a named regression test, testStreamFollowsLiveTrackWhileKeepingStationIdentity in PlaybackReducerTests, written from the live repro where Sonos reported Eurythmics then Prince while the app showed Chaka Khan. Fix, test, and four days of real listening — enough to call it.

features.name: A stopped zone shows what Sorriva last knew, not what the speaker last played
features.desc:
For a zone that is not playing, the reducer returned the stored last-playing outright and never reached the line that returns what polling had just resolved. So every poll resolved the zone's parked URI correctly -- station against the stations table, local file against our database -- and the answer was then discarded.

WHY IT MATTERS MOST FOR EXTERNAL SOURCES: Sonos keeps reporting the URI a stopped zone is parked on, so it can always tell us what a zone last played, including content started from the Sonos app that Sorriva has no record of. Start something externally and it appears correctly WHILE PLAYING (the stopped-zone rule does not fire), then stop it and the card reverts to whatever Sorriva itself last knew for that zone -- possibly hours old and from a different source. Tom's framing: the code is supposed to poll the endpoint, find out what it is, and resolve it -- and it does; the display half was overriding the result.

ROOT CAUSE, and it is an over-correction rather than a design choice: that rule was written to stop the card reading RAW SonosZone fields such as stationName, which polling mutates and which caused the reverting-station and blanking-artwork bugs. Sound for raw fields. But it was written broadly enough to also block the RESOLVED context, which is not raw residue -- it is the URI enriched by our own database -- so the good answer was suppressed along with the bad one.

FIX: delete the early return. The existing final line already falls back to the stored copy, so a stopped zone now shows the resolved answer when there is one and the stored copy only when Sonos cannot describe the zone at all -- a speaker back from a power cut with an empty transport. That is the one job the stored copy is genuinely needed for, and it makes 'self-heals on the next poll' true for stopped zones instead of only for playing ones.

THIRD INSTANCE of one pattern: something the app stored outranking something Sonos just reported. See also bStationTrackFrozenByDeclaration and the grouping ghost fixed in fPlaybackStoreGroupDeclarations.

features.name: PlaybackStore phase C - grouping needs no declarations; Sonos restores the member
features.desc:
CLOSED WITH A NEGATIVE RESULT. The premise was wrong and the behaviour it set out to change was already correct.

PREMISE (wrong): 'an ungrouped zone reports what it played before it was grouped' was recorded as a defect, on the assumption that a separating zone keeps the group's content.

WHAT SONOS ACTUALLY DOES, verified by querying the speakers directly rather than by reading our code: a grouped member NEVER receives the stream. Its transport is set to x-rincon:RINCON_<coordinator>, a pointer at the coordinator, which does the streaming and distributes the audio. The member's own queue is untouched for the whole time it is grouped, and Sonos restores it on separation. Measured: Patio coordinating SomaFM Bossa Beyond (aac://.../bossa-128-aac) with Garage grouped to it; after ungrouping, Garage was STOPPED and parked on its own hls-radio://.../zc7934 (iHeart Lost 80s), not the group's stream. Sonos's own app shows no station for Garage yet pressing play starts Lost 80s -- Sonos does not consider the member to be playing anything, it simply has that URI in its transport.

THEREFORE the pre-existing behaviour was right: what an ungrouped zone reports is what will actually play if the user presses play on it. Tom's ruling: 'sonos ALWAYS is the source of truth.' Declaring the coordinator's content onto a member would make the card describe something the speaker will not do.

BUILT THEN REMOVED: projectCoordinatorContent(coordinatorID:onto:) and its three call sites. It was harmful in both directions -- on joining it overwrote the member's real last-playing with the coordinator's content, destroying the zone's own history that Sonos was about to restore; on leaving, its grace window asserted the group's content for a few seconds before polling contradicted it, which is the flicker that exposed the whole mistaken premise.

KEPT from this work, both worth having on their own: Stop after becomeCoordinator on each separation path, and contentDeclaration(forZoneID:) -- one resolution order (live declaration, then last-playing only while its URI still matches, then the resolved context, then raw synthesis as a last resort) with transferPlayback's three inline branches collapsed onto it. An intermediate version of that resolver put raw synthesis ahead of the resolved context and an ungrouped zone showed correct artwork beside the name 'hls.m3u8', since synthesis reads Sonos's dc:title; raw fields must never outrank resolved ones.

PROCESS NOTE worth keeping: the premise was asserted from reading code and was wrong. Three rounds of fixes were built on it, each producing a new symptom, before querying the speakers settled it in one command. Check what the hardware does before recording a behaviour as a defect.

features.name: Move Swift sources into synchronized folders so new files are picked up automatically
features.desc:
67 Swift files sit at ios/ root and are listed individually in the Xcode project (74 explicit PBXFileReference entries). Only ios/Sorriva/ and ios/SorrivaTests/ are PBXFileSystemSynchronizedRootGroup folders, and nothing lives in them. Consequence: every new source file must be added to the project by hand or the build fails -- and it fails as a missing-symbol error that points at the call site rather than at the project file, so the cause is not obvious. This bit on 2026-08-04 when RadioServiceAdapter.swift was added for the per-service radio adapters; the build failed until Tom added the file manually.

WORK: move the 67 files into the synchronized ios/Sorriva/ folder, strip their explicit references from project.pbxproj, and handle server/swift-config.json, which enumerates the file list and would go stale (regenerate or retire it). Mechanical, but it touches the project file, so it wants a clean tree and a verifying build.

SEQUENCING: Tom deliberately tabled this on 2026-08-04 until PlaybackStore phase B was tested and working -- 'let's table the restructure until phase b is tested and working' -- which it now is. His reasoning for not deferring further: 'definitely better to do it sooner than later before the project grows larger.' Phases D and E both add files, and the UI work will add many, so the cost of waiting compounds. Do it on a clean tree at a known-good point rather than mid-feature.

DONE 2026-08-06. All 67 files moved into ios/Sorriva/; 268 lines removed from project.pbxproj — exactly the predicted 67 x 4 (file reference, build file, group child, sources entry). Explicit references fell from 72 to 5, the remainder being the app product and packages. Verified that each file compiles EXACTLY ONCE: had the old references survived alongside the synchronized folder, every file would have built twice and the link would have failed on duplicate symbols. Git recorded all 67 as renames, so history is preserved. Tom confirmed the build succeeds in Xcode and on device — the check headless xcodebuild cannot make, since Xcode maintains its own index. server/swift-config.json, the retired packaging file list, is dead and its contents now wrong; removal pending Tom's word.

features.name: Station resolution re-runs on every poll for every zone instead of once per URI
features.desc:
Observed 2026-08-04 in a console filtered on CONTEXT: every zone re-resolves its station on every poll cycle, indefinitely. The same zone/station pairs repeat dozens of times -- 'resolved station from URI - Bossa Beyond for RINCON_804AF2A73E9901400' roughly 40 times in one capture, alongside Lost 80s and Yacht Rock Radio for other zones. Each line is a SUCCESSFUL resolve, so the lookup works; it simply runs again next poll.

This is what the resolvedStations cache in PlaybackContextService exists to prevent, and the same churn was reportedly fixed once before (bPlaybackContextResolveChurn -- 'forty re-resolutions of a single station in one log', which is precisely what is happening again). Each resolve reads the full stations table and re-runs adapter matching.

NOT DIAGNOSED. The cache read looks correct on inspection: stationDisplay(for:) computes normalizedStreamKey(zone.currentTrackURI), takes the cached entry only when its stored key matches, and re-resolves only on a nil entry or an expired miss. resolveStationFromURI writes the entry immediately before emitting the log line above. For the cache to miss every poll, either the entry is not landing or the key differs between write and read -- those need opposite fixes and the log cannot distinguish them. Ruled out by inspection: the normalised key strips scheme and query, and iHeart URIs measured directly off the speaker carry no query string, so token rotation is not the explanation. There is only one call site, and observe() is guarded against double registration.

IMPACT: no visible symptom today, but it is wasted network and database work every poll for every zone, and it is why a raw-name flicker was visible at all during the phase C work -- the raw dc:title fallback in stationDisplay only shows when the cache misses, so a working cache would have hidden that class of error. Next step is instrumentation: log the stored key and the computed key side by side on a cache miss.

features.name: Speed up the unit test cycle - 10 minutes per run makes validation too expensive
features.desc:
Tom, verbatim: "Separately, the ten-minute cycle itself is worth attacking at some point - a chunk of it is the simulator boot and test-bundle install, and there's a macOS destination in the scheme that may skip both. Not today's problem, but it would make this whole exercise cheap next time."

CONTEXT. Measured 2026-08-05: a test run that touches a source file takes about ten minutes end to end, against roughly 0.1 seconds of actual test execution (17 reducer tests). Effectively all of it is rebuild, test-bundle install, and simulator boot. A test-only rerun with no source change is far quicker, so the cost is specifically paid whenever code changes -- which is every single time during development.

WHY IT MATTERS BEYOND CONVENIENCE. It directly limits how much verification gets done. Validating that the reducer tests genuinely catch their bugs (deliberately reintroduce each defect, confirm the right tests go red) required one build cycle per mutation. At ten minutes each, the honest recommendation was to validate the subtle tests and take the rest on trust -- which Tom correctly rejected as inspection standing in for measurement. A fast cycle removes that trade-off entirely and makes mutation checking routine rather than an event.

FIRST THING TO TRY: the scheme already lists a 'My Mac (Designed for iPad)' destination. If the test target runs there, it skips both the simulator boot and the bundle install. Not all tests will suit it -- anything touching UIKit or device paths may not -- but the reducer and scanner suites are pure logic over GRDB and files. Worth timing before any deeper build-settings work.

MEASURED 2026-08-08: a plain `xcodebuild build` completes in ~10 SECONDS. `xcodebuild test` scoped to a single suite with -only-testing takes ~10 MINUTES. The tests themselves execute in under a second, so the entire 60x difference is the test target build plus simulator clone, boot and install — not compilation of the app.

WHICH MAKES THE FIX CLEAR: the code being tested is already pure. mergeTopology, PlaybackStateReducer, ArtworkLookup's scoring, ImageDimensionReader and ArtworkBestWins have no UIKit dependency — they are simply trapped inside an app target that does, which forces a simulator. Moved into a plain module they would build and run on macOS in seconds with no simulator at all.

RAISED TO HIGH because fZoneDiscoveryServiceDecomposition now depends on it: that work is explicitly one-step-at-a-time with verification between steps, and at ten minutes a run the discipline becomes unaffordable. Tonight alone this cost six mutation runs plus the ordinary ones.

features.name: NAS share registration with Sonos silently does nothing, and we never read back what Sonos actually knows
features.desc:
MEASURED 2026-08-05. Browsing a speaker's ContentDirectory for object 'S:' returns the shares Sonos actually has registered. On this household that is exactly ONE entry:

    //av-server/media/Test Scan

Lowercase host, and scoped to a subfolder that is NOT where the library plays from (Media/Music II etc). Meanwhile the app's own log shows 'SONOS DRIVER: CreateObject //AV-Server.local/Media on 192.168.1.76 OK' — success returned, nothing registered. So the registration step the app performs before every local playback has most likely NEVER worked, and its success return is meaningless.

WHY REGISTRATION IS NEEDED AT ALL. Sonos pulls local files itself over SMB; the phone is never in the audio path. To read from the NAS the speaker needs credentials for that server, which live in the household's music-library configuration. Sonos appears to match the HOST in an x-file-cifs:// URI against its registered shares to find those credentials. Measured evidence: a URI under Media/Music II played successfully even though only media/Test Scan is registered, so the path scope is looser than the registration implies — but the host must match. 'AV-Server' matches 'av-server' case-insensitively and plays; 'AV-Server.local' matches nothing, gets no credentials, and fails silently (see bSonosLocalHostBreaksPlayback).

THE PROPER FIX: register, then READ BACK. Call CreateObject as now, then Browse 'S:' and take the canonical share name Sonos actually stored, and build x-file-cifs:// URIs from that rather than deriving the name ourselves. Using Sonos's own spelling removes all guessing. If the share is absent from the list after registration, that is a real failure and must surface to the user rather than producing silent no-playback.

DOWNSTREAM — WHERE THIS TOUCHES:
1. LocalPlaybackService.registerSharesIfNeeded (~:178) — the per-zone registration before playback, with its in-memory registeredShares cache. That cache currently trusts a return value that means nothing, and would need to key off the read-back instead.
2. ZoneDiscoveryService.transferPlayback step 0 (~:1689) — registers shares on the TRANSFER DESTINATION. Note it calls ZoneDiscoveryService.createObject directly and bypasses LocalPlaybackService's cache entirely, so the two paths already disagree about what is registered. Both would need to go through one place.
3. SourceResolver.xFileCIFSLocator / sonosHost / sonosNASPath — URI construction. The interim .local strip lives here and would be replaced by the read-back value.
4. AddSMBSourceView manual entry — a share added by typing an IP stores the IP as host. The raw IP was measured to FAIL on Sonos exactly like .local does, and the interim strip cannot help it (no .local to remove). Read-back fixes this case; string transformation never will.
5. Multi-source and multi-share setups — the read-back must match the right entry per LibrarySource, not assume one share.
6. PlaybackIssue — the channel for telling the user a zone cannot reach the share. Currently unused for this; see fSurfaceSonosErrorCodes.

SEQUENCING NOTE: Tom's question, and it is the right one — a newly mounted share will not be in Sonos's list yet. That is fine because WE are the ones registering it: the order is register, then read back, then use. The failure case (registered but still absent) is exactly the case that should raise a user-visible error.

INTERIM STATE: bSonosLocalHostBreaksPlayback ships a .local strip that is proven on four speakers and unblocks local playback. It does not fix manual-IP sources and does not fix the silent registration no-op. This item is the real solution.

features.name: Local playback fails on some zones because the URI uses the Bonjour .local hostname
features.desc:
Local playback failed intermittently and appeared zone-specific: some speakers played, others accepted every command and sat at STOPPED. It also looked like a regression in unrelated work, and an evening was spent bisecting PlaybackStore phase D before the cause was measured directly.

ROOT CAUSE: LibrarySource.host holds the hostname Bonjour discovery produced — service name plus domain, e.g. 'AV-Server.local' (AddSMBSourceView builds it that way). That is correct for the iPhone's OWN SMB connection, which the scanner uses and which resolves over mDNS. But the same field was also used to build x-file-cifs:// URIs for Sonos, which needs the name its registered share uses — the short name. One field serving two clients with different addressing requirements.

MEASURED 2026-08-05, same file, same minute, four speakers:
    host              MasterBath  Office   Workout  MasterBedroom
    AV-Server         PLAYING     PLAYING  PLAYING  PLAYING
    AV-Server.local   PLAYING     PLAYING  STOPPED  STOPPED (UPnP 701)
Raw IP also fails. Percent-encoding makes no difference. A wider gap before Play makes no difference.

WHY IT WAS HARD TO SEE: SetAVTransportURI returns 200 for a bad host because Sonos validates lazily, so the transport simply never leaves STOPPED. The follow-up Play then returns either 200 with nothing happening or 500 with errorCode=701, depending on the speaker. Because .local resolves on some speakers and not others, it presented as intermittent and zone-specific and was variously mistaken for a wedged transport, a share-registration failure, NAS trouble, and a code regression.

FIX: SourceResolver.sonosHost drops a trailing .local; xFileCIFSLocator and share registration both route through it. source.host is untouched, so the scanner and Bonjour discovery are unaffected.

KNOWN LIMITS, deliberately not addressed here: a share added by manual IP entry has no .local to strip and still fails; a machine whose SMB name is not simply its short mDNS name (macOS truncates NetBIOS names to 15 chars) would derive wrongly. Both are covered by bSonosShareRegistrationSilentlyNoOps, which replaces the derivation with reading the canonical name back from Sonos.

PROCESS: this was identified on 2026-08-04 by raw-SOAP testing and then NOT implemented — the recovery was credited to a Stop-before-SetAVTransportURI change made at the same time, and the host finding was treated as a disproved theory. Tom had said plainly that AV-Server worked. A test result that contradicts a dismissed theory should reopen it.

features.name: Surface Sonos UPnP error codes to the user instead of failing silently
features.desc:
Sonos returns a machine-readable errorCode in the SOAP fault body on every rejected command — 701 transition not available, 714 illegal MIME type, 716 resource not found, and so on. sendTransportAction logs the HTTP status and discards the body, and nothing acts on a non-200 at all, so a rejected command is indistinguishable from an accepted one everywhere except the log.

Tom's framing, and the reason the scope is narrow: capturing the whole body is a debugging convenience only. The part with product value is the ERROR CODE, because it lets the app tell the user WHY a zone will not play instead of showing nothing. Today a failed play is invisible — the card shows playing for the optimistic grace period and then goes quiet with no explanation.

That matters more for a shipped product than for development. Tom has a terminal and can query the speakers; an App Store user with a NAS has neither, and a speaker that silently refuses to play is indistinguishable from a broken app.

SCOPE: parse and retain the errorCode, route it through the existing PlaybackStore PlaybackIssue channel (built for this and currently unused for it), and log the full fault body at debug level only. Not blanket logging of every SOAP response.

MOTIVATING CASE: on 2026-08-05 the speaker returned errorCode=701 on every failed play and the app discarded it every time. Roughly three hours went into inferring what that code stated outright, including a bisect of unrelated work. Paired with bSonosShareRegistrationSilentlyNoOps, which is the other half — CreateObject returning OK while registering nothing.

features.name: zone_state was written on every station play and transfer and read by nobody
features.desc:
zone_state cached a station name and logo per zone. It became WRITE-ONLY the moment phase D deleted restoreZoneStateFromDB, its only reader — after which two sites kept writing it on every station play and every transfer for no consumer at all.

SUPERSEDED BY zone_last_playing (schema v20, phase B), which does the same job properly: bound to the URI it describes, and carrying track, artist, isLocal and the album id needed to restore local artwork — none of which zone_state held.

REMOVED: both write sites (persistStationPlay, transferPlayback) and both accessors (updateZoneState, zoneState(deviceId:)).

TABLE DELIBERATELY LEFT IN PLACE. Dropping it needs a migration against real data on device for no functional gain, and it is now inert. Worth doing as routine schema hygiene, not as a fix.

features.name: PlaybackStore phase E - retire the side-channels
features.desc:
Remove the fields on SonosZone that duplicated what PlaybackStore owns, so 'no code path can leave stale state behind' is true by construction rather than by vigilance.

DONE — STATION IDENTITY. stationName, stationNameURI and stationLogoURL removed from SonosZone. stationNameURI existed solely to detect staleness in stationName, a guard against a problem the field itself created. Four consumers moved: the Case 2 change-detection trigger now watches the URI alone (a station's identity cannot change without its URI changing); stationDisplay lost its raw fallback, which is what put 'hls.m3u8' and 'groovesalad-128-aac' on zone cards whenever the resolve cache missed and thereby disguised a cache bug as a naming bug; contentDeclaration lost its raw synthesis, which read dc:title and so could only produce a name worse than none; persistStationPlay stopped writing fields it already declared to the store.

DONE — TRANSPORT OPTIMISM, steps 1-4 of 5. SonosZone.playingUntil recorded the same fact as PlaybackDeclaration.declaredAt in a second place, and had already drifted (5s in one call site, 6s in five others, against declarationGrace of 5). It could not fold into the content declaration because two of six setters make no content claim: pause is transport-only, grouping is topology. So the store gained TransportIntent alongside PlaybackDeclaration. Corrected on the way through: togglePlayPause only graced idle->playing, so a pause the user issued could be reverted by the next poll; it now declares both directions. Built test-first — five reducer tests written before the wiring and confirmed to fail for the right reasons.

DONE — step 5, 2026-08-06. playingUntil removed from SonosZone; fetchTransportStates now simply reports what Sonos said and holds no opinion about what a zone displays. Justified by MEASUREMENT rather than elapsed soak: the parallel run surfaced one real defect (bPhantomPauseAfterTransfer), and auditing every remaining declaration site surfaced a second before it was ever seen (bTransportOptimismScalesWithQueueLength). With both closed, the field had nothing left to cover for.

NOT A STRAIGHT DELETION. playingUntil did TWO jobs: the optimism itself, and a guard stopping the poll clearing a zone's track fields mid-command. The first moved to the reducer; the second still has to exist or a transient STOPPED during a transfer would wipe the track the zone is about to resume. So PlaybackStore gained hasFreshTransportIntent(zoneID:) and the poll asks the store the same question it used to ask the field — a migration, with the answer in one place.

Also done under E: bZoneStateWriteOnly.

features.name: PlaybackStore phase D - demote polling to transport-only
features.desc:
Stop the poll paths writing CONTENT into SonosZone, so the store is the only thing that says what a zone is playing.

SCOPE CORRECTED DURING SCOPING. The spec listed currentTrack/currentArtist among the fields to stop writing. That is wrong and following it would have broken the frozen-track fix: for a stream those come from r:streamContent — Sonos genuinely knows the song — and PlaybackStore.confirmedContent reads them directly. They are transport truth and keep being polled. What D actually removes is the three STATION fields, which are the poisoned ones: Sonos's dc:title is a filename for iHeart, a slug for SomaFM, and the track title for Sonos Radio.

REMOVED: six write sites, and two entire functions that did nothing else. fetchAllStationMetadata issued a GetMediaInfo call per zone on every topology refresh purely to copy that dc:title in — real network traffic for data that had to be defended against downstream. restoreZoneStateFromDB read a zone's last Sorriva-played station and stamped stationNameURI with whatever URI the zone currently reported, forging the very freshness check meant to prove a name belonged to the content in hand; that is the mechanism behind zones reverting to 'last playing minus one', and it ran on every topology refresh rather than only at launch.

THREE VIEWS MIGRATED to the store's snapshots: the group picker rows, the transfer sheet subtitle, and IHeartServiceView's 'which zones are playing this station' check — the last of which compared station names against SonosZone.stationName, i.e. against dc:title, so the warning shown before removing a station could never have fired.

Sequenced views-first: removing the writes first would have blanked them. Verified on device, and the reducer suite confirmed PlaybackStore's behaviour was unchanged throughout.

features.name: Commit the Sonos diagnostic helpers so the technique is not rewritten each time
features.desc:
SCOPE DELIBERATELY REDUCED 2026-08-05 after Tom pushed back: 'sounds like live testing won't use the app? if that's the case then why bother.' He is right, and the original framing oversold this. These scripts do not test Sorriva at all — they test our ASSUMPTIONS about Sonos. Detection was never the problem; Tom notices broken playback in seconds.

THE REAL VALUE IS TRIAGE. What cost hours on 2026-08-05 was not noticing the fault but locating it: our code, the speakers, the NAS, or the network. Claude proposed and had disproved speaker model, share registration, NAS reachability, command timing, encoding, case, iOS flow limits and session exhaustion before measuring. A committed probe answers 'is the contract still true?' in about ten seconds — if yes the fault is ours, if no Sonos changed underneath us.

SCOPE: commit the helper module already written during that session — SSDP discovery, SOAP call, Browse 'S:' for registered shares, read transport state, read a queue. Boilerplate written once instead of six times in one evening. NOT a scenario suite; build scenarios only if something actually asks for one.

If a scenario ever is built, capture-and-restore is mandatory: a probe track left playing on Workout for an hour was read as an album transfer landing there and corrupted a test result.

New top-level directory — needs Tom's approval on placement before anything lands.

features.name: Seeded iOS Simulator so UI behaviour can be verified without Tom's eyes
features.desc:
SPIKE PASSED 2026-08-06 — Tom confirmed the app running in the iOS Simulator SEES THE SONOS TOPOLOGY AND CONTROLS PLAYBACK. Media metadata is wrong, as expected, because that install has no library. Discovery was the one assumption worth doubting (multicast SSDP from a simulator); it works, so the approach is viable and only seeding remains.

SEEDING — REVISED APPROACH, simpler than bundling. The simulator has its own persistent container, so set it up ONCE inside the simulator: add the NAS source, scan a small purpose-built test library. That produces a real database and a real artwork cache by the normal code path, with no export from Tom's phone and no library metadata committed to git. Snapshot the container afterwards so it can be restored if the simulator is erased. This also removes the 'must never ship to the App Store' problem by construction — nothing is added to the app target.

THIS IS THE ONE THAT TESTS THE APP, and where the effort belongs. Tom's framing on 2026-08-05: the Sonos scripts do not exercise Sorriva, so if only one of the two gets built, it is this.

WHAT A TEST LOOKS LIKE: query the speaker for ground truth (transport, URI, queue, r:streamContent), read the simulator's screen for what the app claims (station name, track, artwork, playing state), assert they agree. Works in both directions — drive from the app and check the speaker received the right URI and queue shape, or start something via SOAP and check the app picks it up, which is the external-change path currently only tested when Tom happens to use the Sonos app.

ARTWORK IS A REQUIREMENT — it has TWO INDEPENDENT PATHS repeatedly confused for each other. Local album art comes from files on disk (artPathThumb/artPathFull); station art is a remote logo URL on the stations row. A harness blind to artwork misses exactly what happened this week: station art going nil after a transfer, and a station rendering the previous local album's cover because artAlbum stayed set while only albumName and artURL were patched (the mini player prefers artAlbum). Seeding via a real scan gives the local path for free; the stations rows must carry valid logo URLs to exercise the other.

LIMITS: screen is read as a screenshot, so assertions are visual rather than string-exact — fine for 'Groove Salad' versus 'groovesalad-128-aac', not for exact-string checks unless accessibility identifiers are added. Audio quality, backgrounding and lock-screen behaviour stay out of reach. The simulator is a separate install whose state can diverge from the phone. Automated runs drive real speakers, so the nominated-zones guardrail applies.

BUILT AND VERIFIED 2026-08-06. tools/sonos.py (discovery, transport, queue, registered shares, volume, and a testing() context that enforces the nominated zone list, mutes, and restores prior state even if the body throws), tools/sim.py (locates the app container by metadata rather than a remembered UUID, reads the database READ-ONLY so a running app cannot be corrupted, reads the log, snapshots container and device keychain — the keychain is device-level, so a container-only copy silently loses the NAS credentials), tools/check.py (speakers and app side by side, snapshot/restore). Guardrails live in tools/test-zones.json rather than in memory. Test library seeded in the simulator by a real scan: 95 tracks, 8 albums, artwork on all 8.

Proved itself immediately by catching a UI defect no unit test could see — the scan confirmation dialog being destroyed by the add-share navigation (bScanConfirmDialogLostDuringAddNavigation). The regression suites that run ON this harness are fHarnessRegressionScripts; the instrument is done, the tests that use it are not.

features.name: Single-track local playback pointed SetAVTransportURI at the file instead of queueing it
features.desc:
Playing one local track loaded the track, showed playing, then stopped. It varied by speaker AND over time on the same speaker, so it read as flaky hardware, a wedged transport, a NAS problem and a regression in unrelated work before it was measured.

ROOT CAUSE: playSingleTrack pointed SetAVTransportURI straight at the x-file-cifs:// file. Local content must be QUEUED. Sonos validates lazily, so the direct URI returned 200 and the transport simply never left STOPPED; the following Play then returned either 200-with-nothing or 500 errorCode=701 depending on the speaker.

PROOF: on Workout, which had refused every direct attempt for hours — including Sonos's own verbatim URI from its registered share — a one-track queue played immediately, with a real TrackDuration showing it had read the file header. A three-track queue likewise.

EXPLAINS THE WHOLE PATTERN. Albums always worked because playQueue already queued. Single tracks failed. And transfers failed *depending on what was playing*: a destination inherits whatever the transport holds, so a bare file URI travelled badly while a queue did not.

THE RULE WAS ALREADY WRITTEN DOWN — CLAUDE.md: 'AddURIToQueue (single track, looped) for x-file-cifs://', and the queue flow was spelled out in sorriva-local-playback-arch.md. Claude edited that exact bullet list mid-session without reading the line above it. Tom: 'why aren't you reading our own notes instead of wasting two hours of my time.' That is what prompted consolidating everything into engineering/sonos-playback-contract.md as the single indexed authority.

FIX: playSingleTrack queues the track and plays the queue, exactly as playQueue does. There is no longer any direct-to-file path for local content anywhere in the app.

VERIFIED 2026-08-05: single track direct to a previously-failing zone, then transferred to two other zones. VERIFIED 2026-08-06: albums transfer intact — the last untested combination.

features.name: Phantom pause after a transfer - transport optimism expired before Play was sent
features.desc:
CONFIRMED AND FIXED 2026-08-06, from Tom's device log. The hypothesis held and the measurement is unambiguous: the transfer at 11:42:34.488 sent Play at 11:42:39.737 — 5.25 SECONDS — against a declarationGrace of 5. The transport intent, declared at the START of transferPlayback, had already expired a quarter-second BEFORE Play was issued. The zone then rendered whatever Sonos reported mid-handover, which is briefly not-playing.

WHY IT ONLY APPEARED NOW: SonosZone.playingUntil uses +6s and covered the gap by ~0.7s. The symptom surfaced the moment transport optimism moved into the store on a 5s window (0.0.60). This is precisely why steps 1-4 were shipped with BOTH mechanisms live — the old one masking the defect is what made it a subtle glitch instead of a visible break, and having both allowed the comparison.

ROOT CAUSE, and it was already solved once for the other half: transferPlayback calls touchDeclaration after Play, with a comment reading 'The steps above take roughly four seconds. Restart the declaration's grace window now, so it covers the period where Sonos is settling on the new coordinator rather than having been spent on the command sequence.' Somebody hit this exact problem for the CONTENT declaration and fixed it. When declareTransport was added at the start of the same function, no equivalent refresh was added — so content was refreshed and transport was not.

FIX: declare the transport intent again alongside touchDeclaration, after Play. The window then starts from the moment the command is actually issued, which is the correct reference point — rather than widening the constant, which would only have hidden the timing error.

SAME LATENT SHAPE ELSEWHERE: groupZone also sets its window before its SOAP sequence, but that sequence runs ~2s and stays inside the window. No symptom today; worth remembering if its timing ever grows.

UNBLOCKS step 5 of fPlaybackStoreRetireSideChannels — but only once Tom confirms transfers are clean, since playingUntil is currently still covering for anything else of this shape.

features.name: Remove the retired Swift panel from the Passione hub
features.desc:
The hub still carries a Swift panel that read server/swift-config.json — a file list used only to extract a Swift repo out of the project. That workflow is retired (passione-architecture.md records the hub Swift panel, swift-config.json, deploy zips, iosdeploy and gitops as retired together), and swift-config.json was DELETED on 2026-08-06 as part of the Xcode restructure (fXcodeSynchronizedSourceFolders). Its contents were doubly wrong by then: a stale count, and paths that no longer existed once all 67 files moved into ios/Sorriva/.

So the panel now reads a file that does not exist. Remove it.

NOTE ON LOCATION: this change is in the PASSIONE-HUB repo, not sorriva-app — logged here because this is where it was noticed and where the deletion that stranded it happened. Check whether sorriva-context.html's '32 Swift Files (swift-config.json)' section needs the same treatment.

features.name: Local playback's optimism window was consumed by queueing, so it depended on queue size
features.desc:
FOUND BY AUDIT, NOT BY SYMPTOM — never observed in use. After fixing the phantom pause on transfers (bPhantomPauseAfterTransfer), the same shape was checked in every other place that declares transport optimism, by MEASURING the gap between the declaration and the command actually going out.

MEASURED across 80 real local-playback starts in Tom's device logs:
    10 tracks   1.29s
    15 tracks   2.99s
   100 tracks   4.70s   (window is 5.00s)
Queueing is one AddURIToQueue call per track — roughly 47ms each — so the time consumed SCALES WITH QUEUE LENGTH. The window was opened when playback was requested, before the queue was built, so past about 100 tracks it expires before Play is even sent and the zone renders whatever Sonos reports mid-start.

TOM'S CORRECTION on urgency, and it was right: no album in his library approaches 100 tracks, so nothing was at risk today — the 100-track figure came from a queue, not an album. But 'a queue could possibly grow that long and longer once we implement queue management and playback', which is exactly the feature that makes queue length user-controlled and unbounded.

FIX: re-declare the transport intent after Play in playQueue and playSingleTrack, as transferPlayback now does. This removes the dependency on queue size rather than buying headroom — the window starts when the command is issued, identically for 3 tracks or 300. No constant to tune and no threshold to creep past when queue management lands.

METHOD NOTE: a soak would probably NOT have caught this — it needs a large queue at an unlucky moment. Measuring found it in fifteen minutes. Second defect the audit surfaced the same day.

features.name: Regression suites that actually run on the simulator harness
features.desc:
The harness shipped without anything to run on it. It is an instrument with no tests, which means the code it was built to protect is still protected by Tom looking at his phone.

FIRST SUITE — the playback matrix, in Tom's own words from the 2026-08-04 close: station to station, station to localplay, localplay to station, localplay to localplay, plus last-played restored after ungrouping. He ran that by hand. It is the regression surface for the entire PlaybackStore rearchitecture (phases A through E, v0.0.57 to v0.0.61) and nothing automated covers any of it. Each case follows the harness pattern: drive the app, query the speaker for ground truth, assert they agree.

SECOND SUITE — the scan flows. Add a share, scan, verify track and album counts against the database, and verify the resume path across an interrupted scan. This is the path that produced bScanConfirmDialogLostDuringAddNavigation, and the one where a silent regression is least visible.

What this buys is the ability to re-verify a week of playback work in minutes instead of an evening of manual checking. Runs drive real speakers, so the nominated-zones guardrail in tools/test-zones.json applies; volume is held at zero, which is what makes the hour irrelevant.

Note for velocity accounting: writing these earns their size, but EXECUTING them does not — test-running hours land in owner_hrs with no counterpart on the other side of the equation. Worth settling once whether the traditional-hours baseline (XS=3 through XL=80) is build-only or build-plus-QA, since that is what decides whether both sides are captured in aggregate.

features.name: A TV taking the room left the zone claiming a radio station was still playing
features.desc:
Turning on the TV makes Sonos switch the zone to its HDMI input on its own. Sorriva kept showing the station that had been interrupted — artwork, name, and an apparent playing state — indefinitely. Quitting and relaunching produced the opposite failure: a TV glyph with no words and a music note in the mini player, which was not recognition but the placeholder for having nothing to draw.

ONE CAUSE, TWO FACES. The reducer had no case for external inputs. The declaration went stale (the URI moved on), nothing resolves an htastream URI, and control fell through to the no-blank rule — hold the previous content WHILE THE ZONE IS PLAYING. The zone is playing, forever, with content that will never be replaced, so a rule written to stop artwork flashing between songs ended up guarding a station gone for hours. On a cold start there was no history to hold, hence the blank.

FIXED 2026-08-08. resolveContent now treats HDMI/line-in as a content kind, resolving to 'TV' with a TV symbol and no station identity, ahead of the declaration because Sonos switching inputs is not something the app asked for or can veto. Guarded so a command the user issued within the grace window still wins: without that, tapping a station for a room whose TV is on flashed 'TV' over the station just chosen. The mini player's placeholder was also made HDMI-aware — the zone card already distinguished TV from music, the mini player did not, which is why one surface showed a television and the other a music note for the same zone.

A SECOND DEFECT FOUND IN FIELD TESTING, and the more interesting one: the poll cleared isHDMI whenever a zone was not playing. Which input is selected is a SOURCE fact; whether sound is coming out is an ACTIVITY fact. While a TV warms up, HDMI is negotiated before audio flows, so the playing state oscillates and every poll landing on 'not playing' wiped the input — the card flickered between the TV icon and the last station for the whole warm-up. The clear was redundant as well as wrong, since leaving the input can only mean the URI ceasing to be an htastream URI, which the position-info path already owns.

Seven reducer tests, both mechanisms mutation-validated. Measured Sonos behaviour recorded in engineering/sonos-playback-contract.md section 6a.

features.name: The polling path that feeds the reducer has no test coverage at all
features.desc:
PlaybackStateReducer now has 29 tests and they are good ones. Everything UPSTREAM of it has none: fetchTransportStates, updateZoneFromPositionInfo, and the topology parse that between them decide what a SonosZone actually contains.

That gap has now been demonstrated twice in one day. The isHDMI flicker (bZoneShowsStaleStationWhenTVTakesOver) was a field defect that no reducer test could catch, because the reducer was handling a correctly-flagged zone — the flag was being wiped upstream. A reducer test asserting 'an HDMI zone resolves to TV' passes happily while the poll ensures no zone is ever flagged HDMI for long enough to matter.

These functions take raw SOAP response data and mutate the zones array, so the seam is not difficult: feed captured XML in, assert on the resulting SonosZone. Real responses for the interesting cases are already recorded in sonos-playback-contract.md and easy to capture again with tools/sonos.py.

Worth doing before the next playback change rather than after, since the reducer suite currently creates an impression of coverage the area does not have.

DONE 2026-08-08. ZonePollingTests — 16 tests over parseTopology, updateZoneFromPositionInfo and the new mergeTopology, against five REAL SOAP responses captured from the household with tools/sonos.py rather than hand-written approximations. parseTopology needed no surgery to become testable: it was already raw-response-in, zones-out, merely marked private.

SIX MUTATIONS, FIVE KILLED. Dropping IdleState, disabling HDMI detection, never populating group members, skipping the transport carry-forward, and removing the empty-parse guard were each caught by exactly the test that claims to cover them. The survivor is recorded rather than hidden: disabling the parser's inSatellite guard killed nothing, because satellites arrive as <Satellite> elements the parser never treats as members and are Invisible=1 besides. The guard defends a shape this hardware does not produce — left in place, documented as uncovered.

TWO THINGS THE FIXTURES TAUGHT. The first capture had every zone standalone, so it could not exercise group parsing at all — a second was captured with Workout deliberately grouped into Listening Room at volume zero and restored immediately. And it caught Living Room mid-TV at IdleState=0 against eight idle zones, which turned an assertion originally written as 'idleState || !idleState' — true by definition and worthless — into a real one. A fixture where every value is identical cannot tell a correct parser from one returning a constant.

features.name: Group changes Sorriva did not make are invisible until relaunch
features.desc:
Tom's repro, 2026-08-08: Living Room and Patio grouped playing Lost 80s. Turn on the TV. Sonos ungroups them — Living Room takes the TV, Patio keeps the station — and the Sonos app shows it. Sorriva keeps showing them grouped.

Not specific to the TV. ANY grouping change made outside the app is missed: from the Sonos app, from a voice command, from home theatre autoplay. It persists until the app is relaunched or until Sorriva itself changes a group.

THE DATA IS ALREADY ARRIVING AND BEING THROWN AWAY. refreshIdleStates runs every ~15s on the poll loop and calls GetZoneGroupState — the entire household topology, group structure included — then extracts only IdleState per member and discards the rest. Group membership is set exclusively by requestTopologyRefresh, which fires at startup and immediately after Sorriva's own group/ungroup commands. Nothing observes an autonomous change. The function name hides this: it fetches everything and is named for the one field it keeps.

VERIFIED 2026-08-08 that the payload does carry it: grouping Workout into Listening Room (nominated test zones, volume zero) appeared in GetZoneGroupState within seconds. Also verified there is no second gap downstream — the topology parse sets zone.groupMembers, PlaybackStore copies it into the snapshot, and the views read it. The pipeline is complete; only the refresh is missing.

FIX SHAPE, and the reason it is not simply 'call fetchTopology more often': fetchTopology replaces the whole zones array, which the code already warns can clear zones outright on a timeout, and at a 15s cadence it would contend with the 2s transport poll for ownership of the same array. Extract group membership from the payload refreshIdleStates already parses and apply just that, the same surgical way IdleState is applied now. Network cost is zero — it is parsing that is absent. Rename the function to match what it actually does.

Related: fZonePollingTestSeam. This is the third defect in two days living in the polling path, which has no test coverage at all.

FIXED 2026-08-08, field-verified by Tom grouping and ungrouping from the SONOS APP with Sorriva registering it in under 10 seconds — which matches the design rather than being lucky: the refresh runs every third poll, so 6s while anything is playing and 15s when the house is idle.

refreshIdleStates is now refreshZoneGroupState and parses the whole payload it was always fetching, via the same parser fetchTopology uses, instead of a bespoke regex reading one attribute. THE INTERESTING PART IS THE MERGE. Topology owns identity and structure — which zones exist, their hosts, who is grouped with whom, IdleState. The 2s transport poll owns activity — playing, volume, track, position, HDMI. Neither may overwrite the other's facts, so mergeTopology is a merge and not an assignment. It HAD to be: grouping changes how many zones exist, since a zone that joins a group stops being a zone and becomes a member of one. That is exactly why the old in-place IdleState patch could never see a group change however often it ran.

An empty parse is refused outright — a timed-out or truncated response would otherwise clear every zone in the app, the hazard that kept topology refreshes off the poll loop in the first place. Mutation-tested.

LEFT DELIBERATELY: the full topology refresh that still runs after Sorriva's OWN grouping commands is now redundant. Removing it is a behavioural change on a path where certainty matters more than a round trip, and it deserves its own test rather than riding along with a bug fix.

features.name: Offer the TV input as a source on HDMI-capable zones
features.desc:
A Sonos Amp, Arc, Beam, Ray or Playbar can play TV audio, and its HDMI input is a source like any other. Sorriva has no way to select it. That matters for anyone not using eARC autoplay, or who has TV autoplay switched off: today the only way to put such a zone on its TV is to leave Sorriva and open the Sonos app.

DETECTING CAPABILITY — verified 2026-08-08. The ZoneGroupMember element in ZoneGroupTopology carries HdmiCecAvailable: 1 on the Arc Ultra, 0 on an Era 100. Sorriva already fetches and parses this topology and ignores the flag. isHDMI today is derived from the CURRENT URI, which says which input is selected, not which inputs exist — so a capable zone is invisible until something is already playing through it.

CAVEAT TO CLEAR FIRST: the flag is named for HDMI-CEC, and it has only been checked on an Arc versus an Era. A Sonos AMP is untested and is precisely the case that prompted this. Confirm on real hardware before relying on it. HTSatChanMapSet (present only on a bonded home theatre, listing the surround channel map) is a second signal, but it would not cover an Amp with no surrounds.

SELECTING IT: the input's own URI is x-sonos-htastream:RINCON_<coordinator>:spdif, measured and recorded in sonos-playback-contract.md 6a. Setting it via SetAVTransportURI is the obvious route and is NOT yet tested — a 200 from Sonos does not mean success, so this needs proving on hardware before it is built on.

TVConfigurationError is in the same element (0 on a healthy setup) and looks like a ready-made way to surface a misconfigured TV rather than leaving the user to wonder why the input is silent.

features.name: Read and configure Sonos home theatre autoplay settings
features.desc:
Sonos exposes the home theatre autoplay settings over plain UPnP, readable AND writable, on DeviceProperties. Confirmed against an Arc Ultra 2026-08-08:

  SetAutoplayLinkedZones(IncludeLinkedZones, Source) / Get…
  SetAutoplayRoomUUID(RoomUUID, Source) / Get…
  SetAutoplayVolume(Volume, Source) / Get…
  SetUseAutoplayVolume(UseVolume, Source) / Get…

IncludeLinkedZones is the 'ungroup on autoplay' behaviour: 0 means the TV zone isolates itself and drops linked zones when the TV starts, 1 means grouped zones come along. That is the setting behind bGroupChangesMadeOutsideSorrivaAreNeverSeen — knowing it would let Sorriva EXPLAIN why a group just dissolved rather than merely tracking it after the fact.

UNKNOWN, and the first thing to settle: what string Source expects. Probably 'spdif' to match the input URI. Calling the getters with no Source returns empty defaults SILENTLY and identically on a non-HT speaker, which is how the first attempt looked like 'the settings are not exposed'. Any implementation must distinguish 'not set' from 'asked wrongly'.

OPEN BEHAVIOURAL QUESTIONS from Tom, which need speakers and cannot be answered from the protocol: when autoplay ungroups a home theatre zone, do the departing zones keep playing; if two or more remain, do they regroup with each other; and if ungroup-on-autoplay is off, do the grouped zones actually play TV audio. Worth a deliberate test session — it involves grouping the Living Room, which is not a nominated test zone.

WRITING is a different risk class from reading. These are settings on hardware the user owns and may have configured deliberately, and a wrong write is invisible until their TV behaves oddly days later. Read-only display first; changing them should be explicit, reversible, and show the prior value.

features.name: Decompose ZoneDiscoveryService — seven jobs, one class, one shared mutable array
features.desc:
ZoneDiscoveryService is ~2,300 lines, 39 functions and two delegate protocols, doing at least seven unrelated jobs:
  1. Bonjour discovery — NetServiceBrowserDelegate + NetServiceDelegate
  2. Network reachability monitoring — Network + SystemConfiguration
  3. Topology fetch and parse — GetZoneGroupState, TopologyParser
  4. Transport polling — state, volume, position, per zone every 2-5s
  5. Queue management
  6. Transport control — grouping, transfers, volume with its own debounce
  7. Live iHeart station metadata, which has no business in a discovery service at all

THE STRUCTURAL DEFECT, and the thing decomposition must actually fix: `zones` is a SHARED MUTABLE ARRAY WITH TWO WRITERS. The 15-second topology parse and the 2-second transport poll both write into the same [SonosZone], and correctness depends on each voluntarily touching only its own fields. Nothing enforces it.

THREE WORKED EXAMPLES IN ONE EVENING, 2026-08-08, all the same mistake:
  * isHDMI wiped by a topology refresh — the TV flag cleared as a side effect of refreshing names
  * alphabetical order lost — the sort was a `.sorted` restated at each assignment site, and a new site did not restate it
  * group member volumes reset to 0 — drawn as MUTED while the speakers sat steady at 14 and 18
Each fix was 'remember to copy this field too'. That is not a fix, it is a subscription.

WHY IT HAPPENS: GetZoneGroupState carries almost nothing SonosZone needs. Measured against a real capture, a ZoneGroupMember has 29 attributes and the app uses four — UUID, ZoneName, Location (host) and IdleState — plus group membership from the surrounding structure. NO volume, NO transport state, NO track, NO position. Those come from separate RenderingControl and AVTransport calls on the faster poll. So a topology refresh that writes a whole SonosZone is writing DEFAULTS into a dozen fields it knows nothing about. Volume 0 is not stale data, it is wrong data.

TARGET SHAPE — hold the two apart so the bug cannot be written:
  * topology[id] — name, host, idleState, groupMembers. Written only by the 15s parse.
  * transport[id] — volume, playing, track, URI, position, isHDMI. Written only by the 2s poll.
  * SonosZone becomes DERIVED: a pure function marries the two on demand and hands the result to PlaybackStore exactly as today.

The point is not tidiness. Today the topology writer holds a SonosZone WITH a volume field on it, so it CAN wipe volume — and did, three times. If it only ever holds a struct that has no volume field, wiping volume stops being something we remembered not to do and becomes something that will not compile. Same move as PlaybackStore's URI binding: make the bad state unrepresentable rather than guarded. It also answers 'which fields belong to whom' once, in the type, instead of in a hand-maintained list inside a merge function — which is exactly what failed.

NOT PLAYBACKSTORE'S JOB. Its split is content-truth versus transport-truth FOR DISPLAY. Topology versus transport is a different question — what the speaker IS, before anything decides what to draw. Folding one into the other puts two unrelated reconciliations in the reducer and spoils a split that is currently clean.

APPROACH — ONE THING AT A TIME, Tom's direction 2026-08-08. Remove one function or one related group per
step, isolate the tests to that piece, confirm the existing suites still pass, and commit before starting
the next. A regression then has one candidate rather than seven, and a bisect lands on a small diff. This
is explicitly NOT a big-bang restructure of a 2,300-line file.

ORDER, and the first step is not a file move. Separating topology[id] from transport[id] changes WHO OWNS
WHICH DATA inside the existing class — no new files, no moved code — and it is verified by mergeTopology,
which is already pure and already covered. Do it FIRST: it kills the bug class outright, and every step
after it becomes genuinely behaviour-neutral tidying. Extracting files while two writers still share a
mutable array only moves the bug somewhere new.

Then, independently and in any order: iHeart live metadata (least coupled, plainly does not belong here),
Bonjour discovery with its two delegate protocols, network reachability, queue management, and transport
control with its volume debounce.

SEQUENCING: fZonePollingTestSeam FIRST — done 2026-08-08, and it already covers parseTopology, updateZoneFromPositionInfo and mergeTopology against real captured SOAP. Tests before restructuring, so the refactor has something to prove it did not change behaviour. Do the topology/transport split first since it has three demonstrated failures behind it; Bonjour, reachability and the iHeart metadata can move out afterwards and independently.

fFastUnitTestCycle IS A REAL PREREQUISITE HERE, not a nicety. This approach depends on verifying each step in isolation, and a test run currently costs ~10 MINUTES against ~10 SECONDS for a plain build — measured 2026-08-08. Essentially all of it is the test target build plus cloning, booting and installing a simulator; the tests themselves run in under a second. Seven steps with two or three runs each is four to five hours of waiting, which is precisely how a disciplined refactor degrades into 'I'll just do two at once'. The pieces being tested here — mergeTopology, parseTopology, the reducer — are already PURE and only need a simulator because they are trapped in a UIKit app target.

STEP ONE COMPLETE, 2026-08-08. SonosTopology.swift now holds the pure half — parse, merge and applyPositionInfo, plus SonosZone, SonosGroupMember and the XML parser. ZoneDiscoveryService went from 2,377 to 2,032 lines and keeps thin wrappers, so it still owns WHEN these run but no longer HOW they work. updateZoneFromPositionInfo was split: the parsing became pure and moved, the zone lookup and write-back stayed behind and are covered by ZoneServiceLookupTests. Verified behaviour-preserving by the full hosted suite — ZonePollingTests 21/21 unchanged.
