REMAINING, roughly in order of increasing risk: the Sonos command layer (~12 static functions that send SOAP to a host, no state, currently untested); the polling loop and its timers; the zone topology cache; Bonjour discovery and network-change handling; the user action orchestration (group, ungroup, transfer, volume); and finally the 23 places this file reaches into PlaybackStore, which is the state-ownership question and needs a design decision before any code.

STEP TWO COMPLETE, 2026-08-09. SonosCommands.swift holds all sixteen speaker commands — transport actions, SetAVTransportURI with and without metadata, the four queue operations, createObject for NAS registration, addMember and becomeCoordinator for grouping, volume set and read, position and media info, and verifyPlaybackStarted. 556 lines moved; ZoneDiscoveryService is now 1,515 lines, down from 2,377 before step one — a 36% reduction across the two slices.

MOVED VERBATIM AND DELIBERATELY SO. Unlike step one, this code has NO tests, so there was no way to prove a restructuring behaviour-preserving. No shared SOAP helper was introduced, no sequence reordered, no signature changed; the 41 call sites were repointed and the compiler plus a live pass over play, pause, skip, local queue, volume, grouping and transfer were the verification. Combining the move with a refactor would have made a failure impossible to attribute.

STEP THREE, and the one that actually buys something: a shared SOAP transport as a seam, so a fake speaker can be injected. Every command below currently builds its own URLRequest inline — sixteen near identical blocks of envelope, URL, headers, POST and log. Collapsing them is worth doing on its own, but the real prize is that sonos-playback-contract.md stops being prose that code may or may not still obey and becomes assertions that fail when someone breaks a sequence.

REMAINING AFTER THAT: the polling loop and its timers; the zone topology cache; Bonjour discovery and network-change handling; the user action orchestration (group, ungroup, transfer, volume); and the 23 PlaybackStore references, which are the state-ownership question and still need a design decision first.

STEP THREE COMPLETE, 2026-08-09. SonosSOAP.swift holds one place where a SOAP call is built and sent; all sixteen commands now go through it and no hand-built URLRequest remains. SonosCommands dropped 604 to 371 lines — 233 lines were duplicated envelope, URL, headers and POST.

A REAL DEFECT THE DUPLICATION WAS HIDING: addURIToQueue and createObject set no timeoutInterval at all, so they inherited URLSession's 60-second default. Both run on the local-file path — share registration and queue building — so an unreachable speaker froze the start of an album for a full minute instead of failing in seconds. Nobody chose that; it is what the fifteenth and sixteenth hand-written copies happened to omit. Timeouts are now named (quick 3s, action 5s, bulk 10s) with the reason attached, rather than a spread of 3/5/10/none with no recoverable rationale.

ONE WIRE-FORMAT CHANGE, verified in the room: those same two commands were the only ones sending an <?xml?> prolog. The shared builder does not emit one, matching the fourteen that always worked. Local album playback, pause, skip and transfer were all confirmed working afterwards, which exercises share registration and queue building specifically.

THE SEAM IS IN, THE TESTS ARE NOT. SonosCommands.soap is settable, so a fake speaker can be substituted. What that buys is asserting a single command's XML. It is NOT enough for the sequences in sonos-playback-contract.md — clear-then-add-then-point-at-the-queue, verify because a 200 does not mean success — which need a fake one level up, at SonosCommands itself, where LocalPlaybackService calls it. That is the next piece and the one that finally makes the contract enforceable rather than advisory.

features.name: Zone cards stopped being alphabetical after v0.0.68
features.desc:
Shipped in v0.0.68 and found in the field the same evening: zone cards in Zones, and the transfer and group pickers, were no longer sorted by name.

CAUSE. `zones` is a display-ready list and has always been alphabetical, but that invariant lived as a `.sorted { $0.name < $1.name }` REPEATED AT EACH ASSIGNMENT SITE, plus a comment on the property declaration. bGroupChangesMadeOutsideSorrivaAreNeverSeen added a new assignment site — the 15-second refreshZoneGroupState merge — without it. Because that path replaces the list every 15 seconds, alphabetical order survived only until the first poll, which is why it looked like the sort had been removed entirely rather than missed once.

FIXED 2026-08-08 by moving the sort INSIDE mergeTopology so both callers inherit it, rather than adding a third `.sorted` and leaving the same trap for the next person. Two tests assert the ordering, including one that feeds a deliberately reversed list, and both go red when the sort is removed.

THE REAL LESSON is not 'remember to sort'. It is that an invariant restated at every call site is an invariant waiting to be broken by the next call site, and that a comment on a property does not enforce anything. The rule now lives in one pure function that a test can hold to account.

features.name: A full topology refresh silently cleared the TV flag and a zone's capabilities
features.desc:
Found 2026-08-08 while fixing bZoneOrderLostByTopologyMerge, and it predates that bug rather than being caused by it.

fetchTopology carried its own INLINE COPY of the zone merge — near-identical to mergeTopology but missing two fields. It did not carry forward isHDMI, so any full topology refresh cleared the flag marking a zone as being on its TV input; and it did not carry forward capabilities, which are loaded from the devices table and are not in the topology payload, so they reset to the default set.

The isHDMI half is the same class as the flicker in bZoneShowsStaleStationWhenTVTakesOver: which input a zone is on is a SOURCE fact, and code that clears it as a side effect of refreshing something else will make the Living Room card fall back to a stale station until the next position-info poll restores the flag. It would have been hard to attribute, since a topology refresh is triggered by grouping and by app launch rather than on a timer.

FIXED by deleting the duplicate outright — fetchTopology now calls mergeTopology, which carries both fields, tolerates a duplicate zone id (the inline copy used Dictionary(uniqueKeysWithValues:), which TRAPS on one) and returns sorted.

WORTH RECORDING WHY IT EXISTED: two copies of one rule. The duplication is also what let the sort invariant go missing, so a single deletion closed both. When the same merge is needed in a third place, it must call this function rather than grow a third copy.

features.name: A zone that spent the evening on TV claims a radio station once the TV is released
features.desc:
Living Room played TV all evening. Sonos then released the HDMI input entirely — measured 2026-08-08: state STOPPED, CurrentURI EMPTY, NrTracks 0, PlayMedium NONE. The card immediately showed 'Lost 80s', a station last played hours earlier.

CAUSE. The HDMI branch in resolveContent DERIVES 'TV' from the live zone each time; it is not a declaration. zone_last_playing is written by PlaybackStore.declare, and nothing ever declares the TV because Sorriva did not start it. So while Sonos reports the input the card is right, and the moment Sonos lets go the reducer reaches past it to the last thing that WAS declared.

This is the ghost class the PlaybackStore rearchitecture was built to end, merely delayed by however long the speaker holds the input. Tom's rule from 2026-08-04 settles what it should say: Sonos is always the source of truth, and what a zone last played is what it last played. That was the television.

FIX: persist the TV as last-playing when the reducer resolves a zone to it, so the fallback tells the truth instead of reaching behind it. Touches the store's persistence rules, which is why it was deliberately not improvised at midnight.

PAIRS WITH bPlayOfferedWhenTransportCannotPlay — together they are why that card both said the wrong thing and offered a button that could not work.

CLOSED WITHOUT WORK, 2026-08-09 — the proposed fix was wrong in principle.

This entry proposed persisting the TV as last-playing so the fallback would 'tell the truth instead of reaching behind it'. Tom rejected it: if Sonos reports null for media, then it is null, and filling that null from the app's own memory produces a card offering playback that cannot happen. Measured the same day: after the input was released, GetCurrentTransportActions returned 'Set' alone — the speaker itself says it can neither Play nor Stop. A card showing a station there is not merely stale text, it is a control that lies.

The rule stands as decided during the PlaybackStore rearchitecture: what Sonos reports is what is playing or last played, and the app never substitutes its own account. Filling a null would have reintroduced exactly the app-versus-Sonos contest that several sessions were spent removing.

MEASURED 2026-08-09, and it is why this is an edge case rather than a class of bug: all nine zones in the household, eight of them STOPPED, reported a real URI with NrTracks 1 and Actions 'Set, Stop, Play'. A stopped zone KEEPS its URI, so Sonos can still describe it and the resolver answers from Sonos at step 3, never reaching the stored fallback. The broken state requires Sonos to discard the URI entirely, observed once, after the television released the HDMI input.

The display half of this is absorbed into bPlayOfferedWhenTransportCannotPlay: an empty transport should show nothing and offer nothing, and those two must change together or the result is a blank card with a live play button. Separately, if a 'play what this zone last played' affordance is ever wanted, it must RE-SEND the URI the way tapping a station does — pressing Play on an empty transport will never work, whatever the card says. That is a feature, not a display rule.

features.name: Play is offered on zones whose transport cannot play anything
features.desc:
Living Room, 2026-08-08, after Sonos released its HDMI input: the zone card showed a play button and a station name. Asked what it could actually do, the speaker said Actions = 'Set'. Not Stop, not Play — Set alone. NrTracks 0, CurrentURI empty, PlayMedium NONE. Pressing play would have done nothing or errored; it certainly would not have started the station on the card.

A STALE LABEL IS A DISPLAY BUG. A CONTROL THAT CANNOT WORK IS A PROMISE THE APP CANNOT KEEP, and the user has no way to tell the difference until they press it.

THE APP NEVER CONSULTS GetCurrentTransportActions. Sonos reports exactly what a zone can do right now, and three distinct values were observed in one day: 'Set, Stop, Play' on a normal zone whether playing or stopped; 'Set, Play' with an HDMI input selected; and 'Set' alone with nothing loaded. Sorriva enables playback controls without asking.

This is the same shape as IdleState (sonos-playback-contract.md 6a): a field Sonos has always exposed that answers a question the app was inferring. Honouring it fixes this case and every other dead-transport state nobody has thought of, rather than special-casing the one that was noticed.

SCOPE WARNING: this changes when playback controls are enabled on EVERY zone card, mini player and Now Playing sheet. It wants the transport actions carried into ZonePlaybackSnapshot so the reducer decides, consistent with the rest of the store, and it wants tests — the polling seam now exists for exactly this. Not a one-line change despite the small fix.

REFRAMED 2026-08-09. Only one triggering condition has ever been observed, and a household probe the same day found all nine zones — eight of them STOPPED — reporting a real URI with NrTracks 1 and Actions 'Set, Stop, Play'. A stopped zone keeps its URI, so this is not a frequent fault and the original entry overstated its reach.

It is worth doing as a GUARD rather than as a fix for enumerated cases: the app should not offer playback controls when the speaker reports it cannot play, whatever the cause. That is correct for every unobserved case too, and it costs nothing when Actions are normal. Tom, 2026-08-09: a good guard that accounts for any use case we are not accounting for.

ABSORBS THE DISPLAY HALF of bTVNotRecordedAsLastPlaying, closed the same day. An empty transport must show nothing AND offer nothing; changing only one produces a blank card with a live play button, which is worse than the current behaviour.

features.name: Volume debounce guard in updateZoneFromPositionInfo is computed but never used
features.desc: In ZoneDiscoveryService.updateZoneFromPositionInfo, volumeIsDebouncing is calculated from volumeCommandTimes and volumeDebounceInterval and then never read. The comment above it (B-001) states volume should only be updated from a poll when no recent volume command has been sent, so either the guard was dropped in a refactor or the volume update it protected moved elsewhere and the calculation is dead leftover. Found 2026-08-08 while extracting the pure parsing functions for the fast test suite; not fixed at the time to keep that surgery behaviour-preserving. Decide which it is before deleting: if a poll can still overwrite a just-set volume, this is the missing guard for the member-volume cycling class of bug, and it needs a test. If the volume update genuinely moved, delete the dead lines.

features.name: Transfer briefly shows both zones grouped before settling
features.desc:
Transferring playback briefly shows the source and destination zones as grouped before settling. Reported 2026-08-08, after the timed topology refresh shipped in v0.0.68.

NOT A REPORTING ERROR. Transfer moves audio by grouping the destination onto the source so playback syncs, waiting 2 seconds, then having the source step aside so the destination inherits the queue. For roughly 2.5 seconds the zones genuinely ARE grouped on the speakers. Topology refresh runs every third poll — about every 6 seconds during playback — so it lands inside that window roughly two times in five and correctly reports a grouping that is about to undo itself. Previously topology was only read after Sorriva's own commands completed, so the app never observed the middle of its own manoeuvre.

REQUIREMENT. The timed topology refresh must not run while a transfer is in flight. The transfer already ends with an explicit refresh 1.5 seconds after its last step, so the settled picture still arrives.

CONSTRAINT ON THE IMPLEMENTATION. Suppression must be a self-expiring deadline, not a boolean that is set and cleared. A flag whose reset sits at the end of an async sequence strands every group change invisible until relaunch if that sequence dies — the failure shape of bAutoLockNeverRestored and of bGroupChangesMadeOutsideSorrivaAreNeverSeen. A deadline degrades to today's behaviour instead of to a permanent fault. Measured transfers run about 5.2 seconds; roughly 8 gives headroom.

SCOPE. Transfer only. Grouping and ungrouping must continue to appear immediately, since there the group change is the user's intent rather than a means to something else. Accepted cost: a grouping made from the Sonos app during the suppression window appears a few seconds later than it otherwise would.

FIXED 2026-08-09, verified in the room. timedTopologyPausedUntil is a deadline checked by the every-third-poll refresh; explicit requestTopologyRefresh calls are untouched, so grouping and ungrouping still appear immediately. The pause is armed at the JOIN rather than at the top of the transfer task — everything before it is queue setup that loops over the registered NAS sources, so starting the clock there would leave the window shortest exactly when a household has the most shares — and lifted just before the transfer's own closing refresh so normal cadence resumes at once.

features.name: Assert the local playback command sequence, not just the individual commands
features.desc:
The local-file playback sequence is documented in sonos-playback-contract.md 3 and enforced by nothing. Playing a local file is six commands in a fixed order — Stop, clear the queue, add each track individually, point the transport at the speaker's own queue, Play, then read the state back. Collapsing that into a single SetAVTransportURI aimed at the file compiles, returns 200, and then either sits at STOPPED or fails the following Play with errorCode=701, varying by speaker and over time on the same speaker. Measured 2026-08-05 on Workout.

As of 2026-08-09 each command is tested individually via the SonosSOAP seam, but nothing asserts the ORDER, so the sequence remains protected only by whoever last read the contract.

REQUIREMENT. Drive LocalPlaybackService for a single track and for a multi-track album, and assert the ordered list of commands reaching the transport matches the contract. RecordingSOAPTransport already keeps that ordered log, so the assertion itself is short.

OBSTACLE — A SECOND SEAM IS NEEDED. The path does more than talk to Sonos: building per-track DIDL reads the FLAC header off the NAS over SMB to obtain a duration. A test would otherwise depend on the NAS being reachable, which makes it neither fast nor deterministic. Estimated to be comparable in effort to the SOAP seam itself, and it is the reason this is sized M rather than S.

SCOPE. Hosted suite only. LocalPlaybackService pulls in SMBClient and the database, so it cannot run in FastTests.

RELATED. The same approach then covers the transfer sequence (5) and grouping (6), which have the same property of being order-dependent and currently unguarded.

features.name: Sonos favorites as a library source — the route to SiriusXM, Spotify and any closed service
features.desc:
Sonos exposes the household's saved favorites over local UPnP at ContentDirectory FV:2 — no cloud API, no developer programme, no quota approval. This is the only route to a service whose catalogue is contractually closed, and it is how SiriusXM, Spotify and Sonos Radio become playable from Sorriva.

THE ARCHITECTURAL REASON IT WORKS AT ALL. Sorriva never authenticates to Sonos or to SiriusXM. It relies entirely on authentication already performed in the Sonos app — the credential lives in the speaker, and Sorriva only ever hands the speaker a reference to content the household is already entitled to. That is why no OAuth, no developer registration and no partner status is required, and it is also the boundary of what can be claimed: behaviour is only known for accounts already linked.

VERIFIED, 2026-08-10 and 2026-08-11.
1. A SiriusXM favorite played on a home speaker via SetAVTransportURI with the favorite's URI and its resMD block, then Play — the shape SonosCommands.setAVTransportURIWithMetadata already sends. PLAYING, with live track metadata as 'TYPE=SNG|TITLE ...|ARTIST ...', the format already parsed for iHeart.
2. CROSS-HOUSEHOLD: the same favorite's URI and metadata, taken from the HOME household, played unchanged on a second Sonos system on a different subnet. Verified as an A/B on the same speaker — the home handle (sn=4, home token) and the local handle (sn=3, local token) both reached PLAYING on the same channel. The handle is not enforced; the speaker resolves the service through its own linkage.

CONSEQUENCE — STORE IT VERBATIM. A favorite is portable as captured. Store <res> and <r:resMD> exactly as read, alongside title, artwork URL and service name, and play them exactly as stored. No reconstruction, no per-household profile, no harvesting of sn/flags/token. Record the household id the favorite came from for DIAGNOSTICS only, so a future failure can be traced to its origin — never as a gate on what is offered.

WHAT IS GENUINELY UNKNOWN, and should be tested when the situation arises rather than designed for now: behaviour when the service is linked to a DIFFERENT SiriusXM account, or the households use different SONOS accounts. Both were interchangeable here because Tom's two systems link the same accounts. Since Sorriva performs no authentication of its own, it has no way to detect or repair a mismatch — the failure would surface as a favorite that simply does not play. Worth a measurement if a second account ever exists; not worth designing against on speculation.

BROWSE, THEN CURATE. Sorriva reads the full favorites list and presents it for selection; the user chooses which belong in their library. A household's favorites accumulate for every room and every listener, and the library should hold what this user wants, not all of them.

GROUPING. Present by <r:description> so SiriusXM, Spotify and Sonos Radio appear as distinct services, both when selecting and in the library afterwards.

SONOS RADIO COMES FREE WITH THIS — same shape, sid=303, so it needs no adapter of its own, only a favorite.

SHAPES ARE NOT UNIFORM, and this cannot assume one parser:
- Some favorites have NO <res> at all — 'Discover Sonos Radio', 'Sonos Presents' and 'Trending Now' are browse shortcuts, not playable items. Filter them out of the selectable list rather than offering them and failing.
- Some carry no sid, sn or flags, with a token account of 0.
- Spotify favorites are x-rincon-cpcontainer: — a container rather than a stream. Same mechanism assumed, NOT proven; no Spotify favorites exist at the second location and no test has been run.

RE-SYNCING. Favorites change in the Sonos app over time. The list must be re-readable so new favorites can be added later, and a stored selection must survive its favorite being removed upstream without stranding an unplayable station.

SCOPE. This is the saved-favorites list, not a service catalogue. Browse('0') returns exactly six containers — A: S: SQ: R: FV: Q: — none of which is a music service's own listing; that needs SMAPI, which is partner-gated. A channel that was never favorited must be saved in the Sonos app once, first.

KNOWN WRINKLE. Sonos rewrites the URI on playback: x-sonosapi-stream: goes in, x-sonosapi-hls: comes back from GetMediaInfo. The reverse lookup that identifies a playing station must survive that — a third case for section 3 of radio-service-integration.md.

NEEDS NONE OF THIS: iHeartRADIO and SomaFM. Sorriva has its own adapters and stores real stream URLs, playing x-rincon-mp3radio:// directly — confirmed still working at the second location unchanged. Favorites are the fallback for services Sorriva cannot address directly.

BUILT 2026-08-12 — DATA LAYER AND PLAYBACK COMPLETE, SETUP UI NOT.

Shipped: migration v24 (services table; stations gains serviceId, resMD, householdId; source dropped and its 22 call sites moved); SonosFavorites browse and parse with 12 tests against a real captured response; import writing chosen favorites as stations; three service cards in Settings whose Connected/Available state derives from station counts; the Library reading every service instead of two named ones. SiriusXM, Sonos Radio and Spotify all play from the library, verified in the room.

STATION IDENTITY IS THE CHANNEL, NOT THE URI. Matching on the full URI created two rows for one channel saved in two households, differing only in the account handle the speaker ignores. Identity is now everything before the '?'. Removal is scoped to what was on screen — a channel favorited only at another location is absent from this list, and absent is not deselected.

FOUR DEFECTS FOUND AND FIXED IN THE SAME SESSION, all in code that looked finished:
1. DIDL metadata was interpolated into the SOAP envelope UNESCAPED, in both setAVTransportURIWithMetadata and addURIToQueue. Invisible for months because every caller passed an empty string; a favorite's resMD was the first real content and SiriusXM simply would not play. The tools script that proved favorites work on 2026-08-10 escaped it and the app did not — that one difference was the whole failure.
2. Spotify favorites are CONTAINERS, not streams. SetAVTransportURI at an x-rincon-cpcontainer: returns 500 errorCode 714, and the following Play returns 200 while the speaker resumes whatever was already queued — a success code playing the wrong thing. Containers expand into the queue exactly as local files do; enqueuing one produced 50 tracks and played.
3. Playback fell back to IHeartAPI.fetchStreamURL for any station lacking a cached URL, including favorites, which carry NEGATIVE ids. Now scoped to iHeart.
4. The zone picker announced 'iHeartRADIO' over every station.

STILL OUTSTANDING: the service setup screens. See fServiceSetupScreens.

CLOSED 2026-08-16. The 'STILL OUTSTANDING: the service setup screens' line above was the last item in scope, and fServiceSetupScreens closed 2026-08-13. Everything this entry set out to do is built and verified against real households: reading FV:2, importing chosen favorites, the services table, channel-based identity across two systems, and playback for SiriusXM, Sonos Radio and Spotify.

THE SPOTIFY CAVEAT ABOVE IS NOW RESOLVED. 'Same mechanism assumed, NOT proven' — it is proven: containers expand into the queue and play, and 2026-08-16 the queue's own reporting was measured field by field (see fSpotifyPlaylistIdentity).

WHAT LEFT WITH ITS OWN ENTRY, so closing this loses nothing: per-service identification of a PLAYING station, which turned out to be a distinct problem from importing one — bSonosRadioTitleShownAsStation (closed), fSiriusXMStationIdentity, fSpotifyPlaylistIdentity, and the orphaned-favorite case in bOrphanedFavoriteStrandsUnplayableStation.

features.name: One consistent setup screen for every service — two panes, tap to add or remove
features.desc:
All radio services reach their content through inconsistent screens. iHeartRADIO and SomaFM use a two-step flow — a detail screen listing saved stations, and a separate Browse + Add screen behind a button. The favorites-backed services (SiriusXM, Sonos Radio, Spotify) use a third layout built in isolation on 2026-08-12: leading checkmarks, no artwork, a toolbar Save, no search.

THE BROWSE + ADD STEP IS UNNECESSARY. Selecting a service should present its available content immediately.

REQUIREMENT — ONE SCREEN PER SERVICE, TWO PANES. The upper pane holds content already in the library; the lower holds what is available and unselected. Tap toggles membership in either direction. Sorting happens when the screen APPEARS, not while tapping, or rows move under the user's finger mid-tap.

REQUIREMENT — SETUP SCREENS DO ADD AND REMOVE ONLY. Favorite and Play-on are library functions and already exist there: the Library station card opens a zone picker on tap and Favorite / Play on / Remove from Library on long press. Duplicating them in setup would give tap two meanings.

REQUIREMENT — IMMEDIATE COMMIT. No Save button and no unsaved state. Checking adds, unchecking removes. Unchecking a station currently playing in a zone raises the same warning the Library's Remove does, rather than deleting silently.

REQUIREMENT — SEARCHABLE AND FILTERABLE, as iHeart and SomaFM are today. iHeart's catalogue is thousands of stations, so its lower pane cannot be a plain list — search and genre chips remain the way in. SomaFM (~46) and the favorites services (~12) can present everything.

APPLIES TO ALL SERVICES. The point is that they behave identically; leaving iHeart on the old flow preserves the inconsistency this exists to remove.

Tom, 2026-08-12, after reviewing the first favorites screen: 'all service detail screens should look and behave the same.'

BUILT 2026-08-12 EVENING — ONE SCREEN, ALL FOUR SERVICES. ServiceSetupView is written once and is generic over a ServiceSetupSource protocol; iHeartRADIO, SomaFM and the three favorites-backed services each supply a small adapter (40–110 lines) saying where content comes from and what add and remove mean. All the behaviour lives in the shared screen.

THE DESIGN CHANGED TWICE DURING THE BUILD, both times from seeing it running. Two panes were built as specified, then rejected: on a phone there is not enough height for both, and with no divider they read as one broken list. Replaced by ONE list with the in-library group sorted to the top, then alphabetical or by popularity via a toggle. Tom: 'there just isn't enough realestate to have two panes on this screen.'

SETTLED BEHAVIOUR: tap adds or removes, immediately, with no Save button and no unsaved state. A tapped item re-groups to the top straight away, but the VIEWPORT NEVER MOVES — no scrollTo, no jump. Favourite and Play-on stay out: they are library functions and already exist there (tap a library card for the zone picker, long press for the action sheet). Removing a station playing in a zone raises the same warning the Library's Remove does.

THE TITLE SAYS 'MANAGE STATIONS'; THE HEADER CARD NAMES THE SERVICE. Both said the service name at first, which read as a stutter. Keeping the service on the card leaves room to make it tappable later — switching services without leaving the screen.

THE TAB BAR IS SUPPRESSED HERE. It hides on scroll everywhere else, but this screen has a fixed frame with an internally scrolling list, so it never scrolls and the bar would sit over the content permanently. The mini player is untouched.

POPULARITY IS OPTIONAL. iHeart has cume and SomaFM has listeners; Sonos favorites have no audience figure, so those services show no toggle and are always alphabetical.

IHEART IS THE ONLY SERVICE THAT CANNOT BE HELD IN MEMORY. Its catalogue is thousands of stations, fetched once into an ephemeral SQLite table and queried with SQL by search text and genre. That is why the protocol asks the SOURCE to filter rather than filtering in the view — otherwise iHeart would have to hold its whole catalogue in memory only to filter it a second time. Genre chips come from Sorriva's own AllMusic taxonomy.

STILL UNVERIFIED: the three favorites-backed services. They are wired to the shared screen but need a Sonos system to exercise, and there was none on the network. Also outstanding: the old SonosFavoriteServiceView remains in the file, unrouted, and should be deleted.

CLOSED 2026-08-13. The screen shipped 2026-08-12; what was outstanding was verification of the favorites-backed path against real hardware, and that happened today — Sonos Radio favorites were imported through the shared screen on a live household and played. SonosFavoritesSetupSource is ONE implementation serving SiriusXM, Sonos Radio and Spotify, differing only by descriptor, so the code path is proven; the SiriusXM and Spotify descriptors were not each exercised.

NOTE the two-pane requirement above was superseded during the build: two panes were implemented as specified, seen running, and rejected for lack of height and separation on a phone. Shipped as a single list with the in-library group sorted to the top.

features.name: A zone reports what Sonos is playing, or says Unknown — never the last thing Sorriva played
features.desc:
Tom's rule, stated 2026-08-13: whatever Sonos is reporting is what shows. Period. If Sonos reports something Sorriva cannot resolve, the station reads Unknown — and where the service IS known, the service is named and the station is Unknown. Track and artwork come from the stream.

WHAT WAS WRONG. A zone that could not be identified fell back to the last content Sorriva itself had played. That fallback was written for a zone the SPEAKER cannot describe — one back from a power cut with an empty transport — and it is right for that. It was wrong here, because the speaker was describing the content perfectly well; Sorriva simply did not recognise it. Observed 2026-08-13: a station playing from the Sonos app but absent from the library left the card showing a station that had stopped.

ROOT CAUSE WAS A COLLAPSED DISTINCTION. 'Still looking' and 'looked and found nothing' were both represented by an empty station name, so the only safe response to either was to hold what was already on screen — correct for the first, wrong for the second. StationResolution now has three states: pending holds the display, unidentified says so, resolved names the station. Blanking on pending would flash on every station change, which is why the distinction is the fix rather than simply removing the fallback.

SHIPPED 2026-08-13 and seen live: a SiriusXM channel absent from the library rendered 'Unknown' with the artwork cleared, while the mini player still showed the song and artist the stream reported. Identity is the only thing withheld.

The service name shows only where an adapter claims the URI. SiriusXM and Spotify have none yet, so they read a bare Unknown until fSiriusXMStationIdentity and fSpotifyPlaylistIdentity land.

features.name: SiriusXM adapter — identify a playing channel against the saved favorite
features.desc:
A SiriusXM channel playing on a speaker cannot be matched to the favorite stored for it, so the card reads Unknown even when the channel IS in the library. Needs an adapter, per the rule in radio-service-integration.md.

MEASURED 2026-08-13, and the two observations disagree — resolve this before writing the adapter:
- Stored from favorites: x-sonosapi-stream:channel-linear%3A7a642de7-c33f-a628-efb2-3d94a829d17b?sid=37
- Playing (obs. A):      x-sonosapi-hls:channel-linear%3a9150cc82-af5c-3be3-d170-0e81d87375a8?sid=37
- Playing (obs. B):      x-sonosapi-radio:channel-xtra%3a282bae89-735a-c222-526d-d217cc615681?sid=37

Observation A keeps the channel-linear namespace and changes only the SCHEME, which an adapter keying on the UUID would handle exactly as iHeart's handles nested transport schemes. Observation B is a different namespace entirely (channel-xtra) and would not. It is NOT known whether B is the same kind of content as A — it may be a Sonos-Radio-style SiriusXM channel rather than a linear one. Neither playing UUID matched a stored favorite, so it is also unconfirmed that a channel present in the library was ever the one playing.

FIRST STEP IS A MEASUREMENT, NOT CODE: play a SiriusXM channel that is definitely in the library and capture what the speaker reports. The known-wrinkle line in fSonosFavoritesAsSource already predicted the scheme rewrite; what it did not predict is the identifier changing.

2026-08-16 — A LIKELY ANSWER, from the Spotify measurement rather than from SiriusXM. r:EnqueuedTransportURI reports the URI ORIGINALLY handed to the speaker, which for favorites-backed content is the favorite itself. That would sidestep this entry's whole problem: no need to reconcile the stored x-sonosapi-stream:channel-linear:… with the playing x-sonosapi-hls:channel-linear:…, because the enqueued URI IS the stored form. It is event-only — see fSonosEventSubscriptions. Worth confirming against a SiriusXM channel before assuming it generalises from Spotify; the measurement is one SUBSCRIBE while a library channel plays.

CLOSED 2026-08-17, AND IT NEVER NEEDED EVENTS. The channel id was in the ordinary loaded URI the whole time. Stored `x-sonosapi-stream:channel-linear%3A65f04311-…` and playing `x-sonosapi-hls:channel-linear%3a65f04311-…` are the same channel differing only by scheme, the case of the encoded colon, and the account handle after '?'. The two observations recorded above were not in conflict: `channel-xtra` was a different kind of SiriusXM content, not a second identifier for the same one.

TWO TIERS, because a channel arrives differently depending on who started it. Measured across three zones:
  favorite-started (Sonos app or Sorriva) → channel-linear UUID → exact id match
  Alexa-started → a raw HLS stream with NO id, only a slug in the path (…/AAC_Audio/classicrewind/…) → matched against the station NAME

The second tier is why the channel number had to come off the stored name: 'ch25classicrewind' can never equal the slug 'classicrewind'. The two changes needed each other.

This required a new adapter capability. `matches(uri:station:)` defaults to today's key comparison; SiriusXM overrides it because one channel in two identifier spaces cannot be reduced to a single key by any function. Every other adapter is untouched.

CHANNEL NUMBERS ARE GONE from the library and every screen — Tom's call: the number is Sonos's addition, not part of the station, and Alexa and SiriusXM's own metadata both report the bare name. Stripped at import AND in the setup list, because that list is built from live favorites rather than the library and would otherwise disagree with itself.

VERIFIED ON HARDWARE both ways: Garage started from the Sonos app resolved by id; Office started by Alexa resolved by name.

features.name: Spotify — identify what is playing when the content is a queue, not a stream
features.desc:
Spotify favorites are containers (x-rincon-cpcontainer:1006206cspotify%3Aplaylist%3A...), which play by expanding into the Sonos queue. The speaker then reports x-rincon-queue: as what is loaded, and the playlist's identity appears in NEITHER the loaded URI nor the per-track URI — so the mechanism that fixed Sonos Radio (bSonosRadioTitleShownAsStation) does not reach this case.

Predicted from the stored URI shape 2026-08-13 and NOT yet observed against a playing speaker. Confirm what a playing Spotify container actually reports before designing the match; the queue URI may carry an object id that resolves, or the DIDL may name the container.

Until then Spotify is a correct Unknown rather than a wrong station, which is the intended behaviour of fUnknownRatherThanLastPlayed and not itself a defect.

MEASURED 2026-08-16, and it splits into two halves with different answers.

TRACK INFO IS AVAILABLE NOW, no events needed. GetPositionInfo's TrackMetaData carries the song in full:
  dc:title Billie Jean / dc:creator Michael Jackson / upnp:album Thriller
  upnp:albumArtURI /getaa?s=1&u=x-sonos-spotify%3aspotify%253atrack%253a…
r:streamContent is EMPTY, which is exactly why nothing shows today: with no Spotify adapter the service falls back to r:streamContent. Same shape as Sonos Radio, so an adapter declaring .trackMetadata gets song, artist and cover. ONE TRAP: Spotify's artwork URL is RELATIVE and served by the speaker itself, unlike Sonos Radio's absolute imgix URL — it must be resolved against http://<speaker>:1400 or it will not load.

PLAYLIST IDENTITY NEEDS EVENTS. GetMediaInfo reports CurrentURI=x-rincon-queue:…#0 with CurrentURIMetaData empty; the playlist is named only in r:EnqueuedTransportURIMetaData, which has no getter action. See fSonosEventSubscriptions for the measurement. Once available, the enqueued URI is the stored favorite's own x-rincon-cpcontainer: address, so it matches the library by the existing channel-identity rule and needs no new matching strategy — and where the playlist is not in the library the speaker supplies its name anyway.

OPTIONS CONSIDERED AND NOT TAKEN for identity without events: trusting our own declaration indefinitely (wrong forever if a playlist is started from the Sonos app, the failure fUnknownRatherThanLastPlayed exists to prevent), or fingerprinting the queue on NrTracks. Both are unnecessary now that a real identity source is known to exist.

features.name: Delete the unrouted SonosFavoriteServiceView
features.desc:
SonosFavoriteServiceView was superseded by the shared setup screen on 2026-08-12 and has been unreachable since — nothing routes to it. It still compiles, still carries its own copy of the pre-tick-by-channel logic, and is the kind of file a future session reads and believes. Its FavoriteServiceDescriptor and SonosFavoritesSetupSource live in the same file and ARE live, so the deletion is of the view struct only, not the file.

Noted at close on both 2026-08-12 and 2026-08-13 without being actioned; logged so it stops being a note.

features.name: Polling stops permanently after a foreground + network-reachability restart
features.desc:
Every zone freezes: content stays wherever it was, volume reads 0 and transport reads stopped, on ALL zones at once, until the app is relaunched. Observed 2026-08-16 on the 9-zone household (192.168.1.x). It is not a metadata fault — the zone cards were simply rendering the last state the poll ever wrote.

MEASURED WHILE WEDGED. The speaker reported CurrentTransportState=PLAYING and volume 37 to a direct SOAP query from the Mac; Sorriva showed volume 0 and stopped for the same zone at the same moment. A relaunch restored everything immediately, including per-track updates.

TIMELINE FROM THE LOG, with nothing omitted between the lines:
  21:52:59  poll healthy — 9 zones, every station resolving
  21:53:05  ZONES: Network became reachable — triggering rediscovery
  21:53:05  ZONES: foreground with 9 zones — restarting poll
            (five minutes of silence — no errors, no timeouts, nothing)
  21:56:22  a user-issued play command succeeds normally
  22:01     relaunch — poll healthy again

NO ERROR WAS LOGGED BECAUSE NOTHING ERRORED. The process could still reach the speakers throughout — the play command at 21:56 worked — so this is not connectivity. The poll simply stopped asking. Note the periodic CONTEXT miss-retry lines, which fire every 30s while any zone plays an unresolvable stream, also stopped dead at 21:52:59; that is the clearest evidence the loop itself is gone rather than its results being discarded.

PRIME SUSPECT: TWO OWNERS OF ONE TASK. refreshTask is cancelled by BOTH startPolling() (which then replaces it) and stopDiscovery() (which nils it). A foreground event and a reachability event arrived seconds apart, and that window runs stopDiscovery/startDiscovery and startPolling against the same handle. An ordering in which the cancel lands after the new task is installed would produce exactly this: silence, no error, recoverable only by relaunch.

TWO HYPOTHESES ALREADY ELIMINATED — do not spend time on them again:
1. The iOS network-flow ceiling. Wrong: that ceiling has only ever surfaced from SMBClient leaking sockets during scans, never from SOAP polling, and Tom corrected this directly. Polling uses URLSession, which pools.
2. A scan exhausting flows underneath the poll. Wrong: the scan running in that window was a no-op — 'nothing to scan, every folder already up to date', 0.5s, zero files, no SMB connections opened.

FIRST STEP IS INSTRUMENTATION, NOT A FIX. Add a heartbeat line to the poll loop so 'is the loop alive' is a fact rather than an inference — the loop only logs on change today, which is why five minutes of silence was ambiguous for as long as it was. Two guesses were already burned here; a third should not be.

WHY IT HAS NOT BEEN SEEN BEFORE, probably: it needs a foreground and a reachability transition close together, and most testing has been on the single-zone household where the same window is far shorter. Frequency is unknown and worth establishing before designing the fix.

2026-08-17 — INSTRUMENTED, AND ONE REAL DEFECT FIXED. The poll now logs: starting (and whether it replaced a live task), task entry, exit reason, a heartbeat every 30s, and a warning when a transport pass exceeds 10s. Before this, a stopped loop and a quiet one looked identical, which is why two guesses had already been burned.

WHAT IT FOUND IMMEDIATELY: on EVERY cold start the app concluded the network had just been restored, when it had never been lost. `lastPathSatisfied` begins nil and `nil != true`, so the first satisfied path read as a transition. That called handleNetworkRestored, which discarded the healthy poll discovery had just started and began another. Usually harmless; occasionally the replacement never ran. Fixed: only an observed loss (false) is a restoration; nil is a baseline.

THE FREEZE ITSELF WAS NOT REPRODUCED with full telemetry. It happened once at 19:05 on the build BEFORE the entry logging, showing a replacement task that never reached its first heartbeat — so it was cancelled at birth or during its first sleep by something that does not log. Four background/foreground cycles afterwards were all healthy.

STILL OPEN, and deliberately: the FOREGROUND path also restarts the poll, via the sorrivaAppDidBecomeActive observer. Left alone as the remaining place the failure might still be caught.

ALSO FIXED: the slow-pass warning counted time the app spent SUSPENDED and fired at 25s after every backgrounding. It now ignores any pass that spanned a resume — a warning that cries wolf is worse than none in the log we read to find the real thing.

features.name: A station survives its Sonos favorite being deleted, and can no longer play
features.desc:
fSonosFavoritesAsSource required that 'a stored selection must survive its favorite being removed upstream without stranding an unplayable station'. Only half of that shipped. Re-reading the household to ADD new favorites works — Manage Stations re-reads every time it opens. Nothing handles the reverse: delete a favorite in the Sonos app and Sorriva keeps the station row, which then fails at play time with no explanation.

NOT YET OBSERVED — logged from the requirement rather than from a failure, on the day the parent entry closed, so it is not lost with it. Reproduce by deleting a favorite in the Sonos app and playing the corresponding Sorriva station.

THE DESIGN CONSTRAINT THAT MAKES THIS SUBTLE, and it is the same one that shaped removal: ABSENT IS NOT DELETED. A channel favorited only at the other house is simply missing from this household's list, and must not be reaped. So 'not in the current favorites list' cannot by itself mean 'delete' — that would wipe the other location's stations on every refresh, which is exactly the failure Tom identified on 2026-08-11 before the import was built. Any fix has to distinguish 'gone from the household that owns it' from 'not present on the system I am standing in', which means householdId is the discriminator.

Behaviour on discovery is an open decision: mark the station unavailable and keep it, or remove it for that household only. Ask before building.

features.name: Spotify reports the song, artist and cover art
features.desc:
A Spotify playlist played with no track information at all — no song, no artist, no artwork. MEASURED 2026-08-16 on Patio rather than inferred: Spotify publishes all of it in the DIDL track block (dc:title 'Billie Jean', dc:creator 'Michael Jackson', upnp:album 'Thriller') and leaves r:streamContent EMPTY. With no Spotify adapter the service fell back to r:streamContent, so Sorriva read the one field Spotify does not fill.

THE ROUTING PROBLEM WAS THE INTERESTING HALF. nowPlayingSource asks which service is LOADED, but a Spotify favorite is a container that expands into the queue — so what is loaded is x-rincon-queue:RINCON_…#0, an address naming no service at all. The rule is now: ask the loaded URI first, and only when nothing claims it, ask the TRACK URI. Spotify's x-sonos-spotify: track URI is claimable; a local file's x-file-cifs:// is claimed by nobody, so local albums — which also play from the queue — keep the path they have always had. There is a test asserting exactly that, because this is the one change here that could reach beyond Spotify.

ONE TRAP, MEASURED: Spotify's cover art URL is RELATIVE (/getaa?s=1&u=…) and served by the SPEAKER on port 1400, unlike Sonos Radio's absolute imgix URL. Left relative it is a broken image that looks like a metadata bug rather than a URL bug, so it is resolved against http://<speaker>:1400.

VERIFIED IN THE ROOM: correct song, artist and cover, updating both when the playlist advanced on its own and when the track was advanced by hand.

NOT INCLUDED: the playlist's NAME, which the queue does not report — see fSpotifyPlaylistIdentity and fSonosEventSubscriptions.

features.name: Track listings for Spotify albums and playlists
features.desc:
SCOPE CORRECTED 2026-08-18 — SPOTIFY ONLY. An earlier version named SiriusXM alongside it, which is simply wrong: SiriusXM is broadcast channels with no albums and no playlists, so track listings do not apply to it at all. Its integration is separate, valid and working.

PARKED, at Tom's direction. Spotify is no longer the direction — Apple Music reaches its whole catalogue and returns album track listings from a public endpoint (see fMusicKitAdapter), so the learned-by-playing workaround exists only for a service we are stepping away from. Keep the measurements below; do not build on them without a reason.

SCOPE — Tom, 2026-08-18: THIS IS SONOS-FAVORITES ONLY. It was written as though learning-contents-by-playing were a platform mechanism; it is not, and it must not be applied to services Sorriva has not looked at yet. It is a workaround for exactly one situation: a service that will not list its own containers and is reachable only through Sonos favorites — today Spotify and SiriusXM.

WHERE A REAL API EXISTS, USE IT. Apple Music will simply return an album's tracks (fMusicKitAdapter), so none of the below applies there. If Apple Music becomes the direction, this entry may not be worth building at all — it exists because Spotify closed its catalogue, not because the problem is general.

An album or playlist imported from a service shows as a single tile with no contents. Sonos knows the tracks; Sorriva does not ask. Tom's order for this work, 2026-08-17: (1) get the track data, (2) integrate into the album view. The same data serves playlists, so both follow from one mechanism.

MEASURED 2026-08-17, and this is what makes it possible at all:
- BROWSING A CONTAINER DIRECTLY IS IMPOSSIBLE. ContentDirectory Browse on the container object id (1006206cspotify%3Aplaylist%3A…) returns 500 / errorCode 701 'no such object', in both BrowseDirectChildren and BrowseMetadata, with and without the numeric prefix. Service catalogues need SMAPI, which is partner-gated. Do not spend time re-testing this.
- BROWSING THE QUEUE WORKS COMPLETELY. Once a container is loaded on a speaker, Browse Q:0 returns every track with dc:title, dc:creator, upnp:album and upnp:albumArtURI. Verified on Patio: 50 tracks, full metadata on each.

SO CONTENTS ARE LEARNED BY PLAYING. The first time an album or playlist is played, read the queue and persist the track list against that row; thereafter it has contents whether or not anything is playing. That is the only route available, and it is a reasonable one — but it means a NEWLY imported album has no track list until first play, and the UI must not pretend otherwise.

THEN THE LIBRARY SECTION. Albums belong with albums and playlists with playlists — in the rows AND in the See-all screens; an item on one and not the other reads as a bug (Tom, 2026-08-17). Playlists already route correctly. ALBUMS DO NOT: they are still shown under Radio, because the Albums section is built entirely on local `Album` records with their own sorting and a detail screen that lists tracks, and a service album has neither until step 1 lands. `RadioRow.kinds` carries `.album` temporarily with a comment saying exactly when to remove it — that placement is deliberate and wrong, chosen because invisible is worse than misplaced.

MIXED SOURCES PER MEDIA TYPE IS THE FOUNDATION, not an accommodation. Tom, 2026-08-17: knowing the SOURCE of an item is what determines which actions are possible against it and whether it is available at all — the NAS being reachable, the internet, Sonos. A local album and a Spotify album sit in the same section and offer different actions. See the target architecture docs and fPlaybackConductor; do not design this as a special case for Spotify.

DEPENDS ON NOTHING NEW. The queue read already exists in PlaybackContextService.fetchSonosQueue for local files; this generalises it and persists the result.

features.name: Per-song artwork, and separating where the song text comes from
features.desc:
Sonos Radio and Spotify show a cover per song; SiriusXM showed none. The cause was a modelling mistake of mine, not a missing feature: `NowPlayingSource` treated 'where does the song text come from' and 'is there artwork' as ONE either/or choice, so every service had to be one of two shapes. SiriusXM is neither — the song text is in `r:streamContent` while the cover is in `upnp:albumArtURI` — so choosing streamContent for it silently discarded the artwork.

The two are now separate questions. `providesTrackArt` defaults to FALSE rather than reading the field for everyone: iHeart publishes none and SomaFM's has never been checked for whether it is a per-song cover or its channel logo, and turning it on blind would replace curated station art.

A REGRESSION I INTRODUCED AND THEN FIXED, worth recording because it will recur with the next service. SiriusXM serves artwork over PLAIN HTTP. App Transport Security allows HTTP only on the local network, so the image was blocked and the card went BLANK — worse than before, because per-song art outranks the station logo and accepting the URL discarded a logo that would have displayed. Upgraded to https rather than dropped, after verifying the same host answers over TLS with the byte-identical image (albumart.siriusxm.com, 24,806 bytes either way). Local HTTP from the speaker itself still passes — that is how Spotify's covers arrive.

RESIDUAL RISK, stated: a host serving no TLS will render blank, the same as today. If a service turns up whose art host is HTTP-only, drop its URL rather than weakening transport security.

Also measured: SiriusXM's metadata is INTERMITTENT — 60s of polling returned no song text and no artwork at all. Absence is normal and falls back to the station logo.

features.name: Albums, playlists and broadcasts told apart
features.desc:
Every imported favorite was a 'station', so an album, a playlist and a radio channel sat in one undifferentiated list while the Sonos app separated them properly. Sonos has always said which is which, in `upnp:class`, and Sorriva discarded it.

Measured across 47 favorites 2026-08-17:
  object.container.playlistContainer   → playlist
  object.container.album.musicAlbum    → album
  object.item.audioItem.audioBroadcast → broadcast

THE CLASS IS NESTED AND ENCODED, which is the whole subtlety. Each favorite carries an OUTER `object.item.sonos-favorite` in plain text; the class describing what it POINTS AT is inside the resMD and entity-encoded, so a literal search over the item finds only the useless one. The first implementation did exactly that and classified everything as unknown; four unit tests caught it immediately.

A SECOND BUG THE TESTS DID NOT CATCH, because they cover the parser and not the database write: the kind was added to the UPDATE path of the import but not the INSERT path, so rows that already existed were backfilled and looked correct while anything NEWLY imported took the default and landed as unknown. Two Spotify albums did precisely that and Tom spotted it. Fixed, plus a second migration for rows that fell in the window.

LIBRARY ROUTING, partly. Radio now shows broadcasts only, and Playlists is a real row with its own See-all instead of a 'create a playlist' stub. ALBUMS ARE NOT DONE: they still ride in Radio, because the Albums section is built on local `Album` records with their own sorting and a detail screen listing tracks, and a service album has no track list until it has been played. That placement is deliberate and wrong — invisible would be worse than misplaced — and `RadioRow.kinds` carries a comment saying exactly when to remove it. See fAlbumAndPlaylistContents.

Unrecognised classes stay `unknown` and ride with the broadcasts rather than being guessed into a group.

features.name: A muted zone looks normal in Sorriva — mute is never read, and Sorriva's own mute is volume zero
features.desc:
Sorriva had no concept of Sonos's mute switch, so a muted zone was invisible and unfixable from the app.

WHAT HAPPENED. Tom started Bossa Beyond on the Living Room from Sorriva. Playback ran, Sorriva showed a volume of 10 and an un-slashed speaker icon, and no sound came out. All five Living Room speakers were reporting Mute=1 at Volume=10 (Arc Ultra 192.168.1.219, two Era 300s, two Era 100s). Sorriva had no way to show it and no way to undo it.

ROOT CAUSE. Sonos keeps volume and mute as two independent things. Sorriva only ever read GetVolume — GetMute appeared nowhere in the app, and neither SonosZone nor SonosGroupMember had a field to hold it. VolumeControlView inferred mute as `volume == 0`, which is wrong in both directions: a speaker muted at 10 drew as fine at 10, and a slider legitimately dragged to 0 drew as muted when it was not.

AND THE MUTE BUTTON WAS A DIFFERENT THING WEARING THE SAME CLOTHES. Sorriva's mute set every speaker's volume to 0 and kept the previous levels in view state to restore on unmute. That was a private definition of mute: invisible to the Sonos app and to Alexa, lost if the app was killed while muted, and — the reason it had to go — incapable of REPRESENTING a mute set by anything other than Sorriva. Pressing it on the genuinely muted Living Room would have raised the volume and still produced no sound.

THE FIX, in three parts, built and verified 2026-08-18:
  1. READ IT. The zone poll asks GetMute alongside GetVolume, for group coordinators and for each member. `muted` is a real field on SonosZone and SonosGroupMember, included in equality and preserved across topology merges — without that last part a fresh member arrives unmuted and the slash flickers off a silenced speaker on every merge, the same defect member volumes had on 2026-08-08.
  2. SHOW IT. isMuted reads the speaker's actual state rather than inferring it from the level.
  3. USE IT. The mute button calls Sonos's SetMute. Sonos preserves the volume across a mute, so the remember-and-restore bookkeeping was deleted rather than reimplemented. Mute now means the same thing in Sorriva, the Sonos app and Alexa.

VERIFIED. GetMute/SetMute round trip against the Workout speaker (0 → set 1 → reads 1 → restored to 0), confirmed by reading the state back rather than by the 200. Tom confirmed the fix in the room.

features.name: Shuffle and repeat on Now Playing
features.desc:
Shuffle and repeat controls in the Now Playing transport row, driving Sonos SetPlayMode. Built and verified against the speakers 2026-08-19.

WHAT SHIPPED. Two controls flanking the existing transport buttons — shuffle, and repeat cycling off -> all -> one. White when active, sHighlight when available but off. OMITTED ENTIRELY, not disabled, when the loaded content has no queue, so radio looks exactly as it did before. Live state is read for the zone on screen only, polled every 3s while that screen is open, which is one SOAP call rather than a fourth call per zone across the household. Taps update optimistically with a 3s debounce, the same shape as volume.

THE MODEL. Sonos keeps shuffle and repeat as ONE field with six values; Sorriva presents two switches and maps between them in one pure function (PlayMode.swift, symlinked into FastTests). The trap the tests guard: Sonos's SHUFFLE means shuffle + repeat-ALL, and shuffle alone is SHUFFLE_NOREPEAT.

MEASURED, all recorded in sonos-playback-contract.md 14: a queue must already be loaded or SetPlayMode is refused with errorCode 712, so the mode is set AFTER SetAVTransportURI; NORMAL is the only value accepted on an empty queue; shuffle shuffles the successor order and always starts on the first queue item, so a controller wanting a random start must Seek itself; GetPositionInfo's Track field is a sequence counter, not a queue slot, and reading it to detect shuffle reports that shuffle is off.

STICKINESS AND THE RESET. Play mode is sticky speaker state and survives a full queue reload, so shuffling one album would silently shuffle the next thing played. Tom's rule is that shuffle and repeat last only for the queue they were set for, so removeAllTracksFromQueue now appends SetPlayMode(NORMAL) — the one choke point every load path shares. SonosEndpointDriver's duplicate queue clear was collapsed into it so the rule cannot drift, the same failure that lost the zone sort in v0.0.68.

TRANSFERS NEEDED NO CODE. Measured: the coordinator handover carries play mode along with the queue and overwrites whatever the destination had, so shuffle already survives a transfer.

DEFERRED by decision: album detail, playlist detail and the zone picker get no controls until the queue concept exists.

features.name: No track has any audio quality data — bitrate and sample rate are never stored
features.desc:
MEASURED 2026-08-19 against the real scanned library, not inferred from code: 95 tracks, 0 with bitrate, 0 with sampleRate, 95 with fileSize, 81 with duration.

The fields exist on Track and are passed to every constructor call, but meta.bitrate and meta.sampleRate are NEVER ASSIGNED anywhere in SMBScanner. bitDepth has no column at all — it exists only on MusicDomain.AudioProperties, which nothing writes. So the Library knows a track is flac and how many bytes it is, and cannot tell 16/44.1 from 24/192. For a product positioned on audiophile honesty that is the gap, and bit depth was only its visible part.

The data is one line away in both parsers. The FLAC reader decodes bytes 10-12 of STREAMINFO for the sample rate to compute duration and discards it (SMBScanner.swift:1214); bitsPerSample is packed into those same three bytes. The WAV reader does the same with the fmt chunk and its own comment documents where bitsPerSample sits without ever reading it (SMBScanner.swift:1022).

FIX: add a bitDepth column; store sample rate and bit depth for FLAC (STREAMINFO), WAV (fmt) and AIFF (COMM); derive bitrate from size / duration. Lossy formats deferred — bit depth is meaningless there and bitrate needs its own work. Existing libraries show nothing until a rescan.

PREREQUISITE for fTrackQualityDisplay: the quality tier cannot be derived from the file extension, because a .flac may be 16/44.1 or 24/192.

Touches the scanner, so PROPOSE THE HOSTED SUITE — this is exactly the case the fast suite cannot see.

features.name: Show track quality — tiers to scan, numbers to read
features.desc:
Sonos shows a bare 'Lossless' label from Apple Music and nothing at all for local playback. Sorriva should do better, for the audience that knows the difference.

AGREED 2026-08-19. STORE THE MEASURED FACTS, DERIVE THE LABEL AT DISPLAY TIME. Never store the tier: a stored tier is a second source of truth that can drift from the numbers behind it, and moving a boundary later becomes a migration instead of a one-line change.

TIERS: Hi-Res (lossless, and 24-bit or above 48kHz); Lossless (16/44.1 or 16/48); Lossy, which carries its rate in the badge — 'Lossy 320' — because there the rate IS the distinction, while two 16/44.1 files are not meaningfully different; Unknown, which is the honest state of the library today.

CONSEQUENCES of the Lossy form: a VBR file yields an average rather than a rate, so round it rather than printing a precise-looking number that moves if the derivation changes; and 'Lossy 320' is roughly twice the width of 'Hi-Res', which the row layout must allow for.

Full numbers belong somewhere reachable — the audience knows what 24/96 means and the tier is for scanning, not a substitute.

PLACEMENT IS TBD (Tom, 2026-08-19) — album or playlist header, per track row, Now Playing, or a combination. Deliberately open: a UI question to answer during the UI work. Nothing downstream is blocked, because every placement is served by the same stored facts.

Depends on bAudioQualityNeverCaptured; there is no data to display until that is fixed. See apple-music-library-model.md 5c.

features.name: Measure what Sonos actually renders, versus what the file is
features.desc:
A MEASUREMENT PASS, not a feature. No code.

What matters to this buyer is not only what the file is but what reaches the speaker. A 24/192 FLAC does not arrive at a Sonos as 24/192 — the speaker converts, and the ceiling varies by model. Showing both would be something neither Sonos nor Apple does, and it is what the 'signal path' idea in the codebase was reaching for. The only trace of it today is a comment on sBrass reading 'Premium moments, signal path hi-res'.

UNMEASURED. Do not design from the commonly-repeated figures about Sonos limits — that is the mistake the playback contract exists to prevent. Answerable the same way section 14 was answered: play known 24/96 and 24/192 files to a nominated zone at zero volume and ask the speaker what it is actually rendering.

Findings go to sonos-playback-contract.md. This decides whether 'what you are hearing' is a real feature or an assumption, and it should happen before any signal-path UI is specified.

features.name: Discover becomes a hub of services
features.desc:
SHIPPED 2026-08-20, and it grew far past the S it was sized at. Scoped as a pure-UI slice that "decides nothing about data", it absorbed MusicKit integration, the track-level play surface, Apple playlists and artist browse — four slices of fMusicKitAdapter — because Tom took each one in turn once the previous worked.

WHAT SHIPPED.
  - Discover is a hub of services. Apple Music live; Tidal and Qobuz dimmed as coming. SiriusXM, Sonos Radio and Spotify are deliberately ABSENT: Tom's rule is that discovery needs direct API access, and those three can only surface what is already a Sonos favorite. iHeart and SomaFM do have APIs and could join — he is still deciding.
  - The Apple Music screen searches artists, albums, songs and playlists, laid out as SHELVES with See all, matching the Library's own rows rather than a filter bar.
  - Artist pages with a full-bleed hero, About, Albums, Singles & EPs, Compilations, Top Songs (horizontally paging, 3 rows), Appears On, Playlists and Similar Artists.
  - Playlist detail, album detail, song-to-album navigation. Tap navigates; long press opens the context menu carrying Play on...
  - Discover is kept mounted across tab switches, so search, results and navigation depth survive leaving the tab.

MUSICKIT REPLACED THE PUBLIC ENDPOINT ENTIRELY, and it fixed a measured defect rather than being a tidy-up. The public API reads the iTunes STORE catalogue, which disagrees with Apple Music's — the album that reported 11 tracks and returned none. MusicKit also carries artist artwork, which the public artist search has no field for at all, and playlists, which it cannot return at all: entity=playlist is rejected outright. Confirmed with Apple's own engineers' statements that catalogue search needs NO subscription and NO signed-in Apple ID, and that the permission prompt is shown once and remembered.

THREE BUGS OF MINE THAT TOM CAUGHT, all the same shape — my code quietly narrowing Apple's data:
  1. Asking for four types in ONE MusicCatalogSearchRequest makes Apple collapse the per-type results. "Pat Metheny" returned 1 artist where Apple Music showed 3. Four separate concurrent requests fixed it.
  2. Apple caps a request at 25 and pages beyond it; not paging looked like Apple having less.
  3. Then paging deep without filtering pulled in records the artist is not credited on at all. Tom: "it only delivers albums where pat metheny is listed." Search results now narrow on the credit; the ARTIST page does not need to, because albums and appearsOnAlbums are separate relationships and Apple has already done it properly.

ORDERING WAS DECIDED BY A CONSTRAINT, not a preference. Tom asked for alphabetical; alphabetical forces every result to be in hand before the first row can draw, and makes paged results insert into the middle of the list under the reader. Relevance order appends, so it pages on scroll like Apple Music and Sonos do. He chose relevance once the trade was visible.

NOT IN THIS: shuffle and repeat on album and playlist detail, still deferred with fShuffleRepeat until the queue concept exists; anything that persists, which waits on fSourceNormalizedSchema.

features.name: One library model, source flagged on the media
features.desc:
The load-bearing slice for Apple Music in the Library, and for every source after it. Full design in apple-music-library-model.md.

Tom's framing, 2026-08-19: one model, with the source flagged on the media, normalized rather than flat — common album/track/playlist tables joined to a source-specific table holding that source's own playback data.

SHAPE: albums and tracks keep only what is true of all music; local_albums / local_tracks hold file path, format, size, bitrate, sample rate, bit depth; apple_albums / apple_tracks hold catalogue id, storefront, streamable. THE FOREIGN KEY LIVES IN THE CHILD pointing back at the parent, not a key per source on the main table — so adding Qobuz later is one new table and zero changes to tracks, albums, or any query reading them.

ALREADY IN PLACE: sourceId exists on both albums and tracks, so the flag itself is built. artists has no source or file columns and needs no change at all.

PLAYLISTS ARE GREENFIELD — no playlist tables exist; today's Playlists row is stations rows with kind=playlist, Sonos favorites wearing a label. Header table plus a join table carrying playlistId, trackId and position. The key cannot sit on the track row: one key per track allows a track in exactly one playlist. Mixed-source playlists then need no special handling anywhere — a playlist item points at a track, the track knows its source, the child table knows how to address it.

THE RISK IS LOCAL, NOT APPLE. Apple Music is purely additive. Moving local files into local_tracks touches SMBScanner, LocalPlaybackService, GRDBLibraryRepository and the artwork passes — working code, against a library that took hours to scan. Mitigation, in order: read through a join view first so the reads are proven before any column moves; run the hosted suite; baseline snapshot outside the repo. Additive per I-008 — create, copy, drop the old columns only once nothing reads them.

Should START a session rather than end one.

features.name: Availability — what can actually play, right now
features.desc:
AGREED IN PRINCIPLE 2026-08-19, unbuilt. Full design in availability-model.md.

Tom's framing: because every row carries its source, reachability is derivable — at home with no internet, service media is disabled; away from home, local media is unavailable. This replaces a weaker earlier proposal to show a warning badge on service content. A badge describes; this decides.

THE ASYMMETRY IS THE POINT. Local music needs the household network and not the internet. Service music needs the internet and does not care which network you are on. Neither condition is 'online'.

NEEDS TWO THINGS THAT DO NOT EXIST: a notion of 'am I on the household network', distinct from 'do I have a connection' and routinely conflated with it (NetworkIdentity.swift is the likely home); and a per-item availability state the UI reads rather than every call site recomputing the rule inline. The dormant MusicDomain.RepresentationAvailability already models exactly this, including the unknown state that matters on a cold launch before discovery has answered.

BOUNDARIES: unavailable means visibly unavailable, not hidden — a user should find the album and be told why it cannot play, not conclude it is gone. This is availability, not quality; they are separate facts and separate indicators. It applies to a powered-off NAS at home just as much as to travel.

Applies to every source, not only Apple Music.

features.name: Canonical identity tables were created, backfilled, and then never used
features.desc:
The v13_canonical_identity migration created music_artists, music_albums, music_tracks, track_representations and legacy_track_map, and backfilled every existing track into them. MusicDomain.swift has the matching types, including RepresentationKind.appleMusic and a locator field.

NOTHING READS ANY OF IT. The entire app runs on the legacy albums/tracks tables; LegacyMusicMapper is the only file that touches the canonical side, and only to translate ids. Found 2026-08-19 while designing fSourceNormalizedSchema.

WHY IT MATTERS: a backfilled copy of the library that nothing maintains will drift from the real one, and someone will eventually find it and trust it. It also makes the architecture docs read as describing a live model when they describe a dormant one.

DECIDE AND ACT: finish it or delete it. Note that fSourceNormalizedSchema is a better expression of the same idea — one table per source with properly typed columns, rather than one generic table with a locator string that has nowhere to put a catalogue id. So the likely answer is to delete these and let the normalized schema supersede them, but that is a decision, not an assumption.

Separate job. Deliberately not folded into the Apple Music work.

features.name: Apple Music — what the screen shows before you search
features.desc:
AGREED TO DESIGN 2026-08-20, unbuilt and undesigned. Today the Apple Music screen is an empty state until you type, which wastes the most valuable screen in Discover.

Tom's framing: "will probably fill the default music page with more stuff eventually", and he chose to design it properly rather than bolt on a recent-searches list. Recents was the immediate idea and is a candidate, not the answer.

CANDIDATES, none decided: recent searches; browse by genre; new releases; charts; Apple's editorial playlists; artist stations. Each is a different MusicKit call and some may not exist there at all — check the SDK interface before designing around any of them, the way the artist shelves were checked.

NOT a search-results question. This is the screen BEFORE a search, which is why it is separate from the search-design work.

features.name: Removing one album from the Library dashboard deletes every track on that source
features.desc:
FOUND 2026-08-20 while tracing the favorites mechanism. Not introduced this session — pre-existing, and it destroys data.

LibraryView.swift:930, the Remove from Library action on an album card, calls deleteTracks(sourceId: album.sourceId) — which is DELETE FROM tracks WHERE sourceId = ?, every track from that entire library source, not that album. deleteOrphanedAlbums() then removes all of its albums too. The confirmation says only "This removes it from your Sorriva library."

So removing one album from the dashboard can wipe a scanned NAS library that took hours to build, with no warning that says so.

AlbumsView.swift:97 does the SAME action correctly, via LibraryService.removeAlbum, which deletes that album's tracks and then the album. Two buttons for one action, behaving differently. The dashboard path also bypasses LibraryService and issues raw SQL, which is how it drifted.

FIX: route the dashboard through LibraryService.removeAlbum like AlbumsView does. Check the track branch at :936 while there — it is correct but also bypasses the service.

features.name: Artist biographies — MusicKit cannot supply them, so they come from elsewhere
features.desc:
RESOLVED 2026-08-21, by replacing the source rather than fixing the code.

MUSICKIT DECLARES Artist.editorialNotes AND NEVER FILLS IT. Measured both ways: on the Simulator with no Apple account at all, and on Tom's iPhone with a live subscription. Nil for artists AND for albums, from the search path and the resource path alike. The SDK confirms there is no way to ask for it — every requestable Artist property is a relationship, and the only MusicExtendedAttributeProperty in the whole of MusicKit is `audioVariants`, on Album and Song. Apple's own web page carries a bio for the same artist, so the data exists and MusicKit simply does not return it.

ONE REAL BUG OF OURS WAS FOUND AND FIXED ALONG THE WAY and did not resolve it: the notes were read only off the relationship-loaded copy, so a failed relationship fetch took the biography with it. Now read from the base artist first and only ever upgraded.

WHY IT MATTERED BEYOND APPLE — Tom: bios are "required as well for local playback". An Apple-only source was never going to serve a NAS FLAC anyway. Superseded by fArtistBiographies, which is source-agnostic by construction.

features.name: Artist biographies, from sources that work for every source of music
features.desc:
SHIPPED 2026-08-21. Artist pages carry a real biography, and it is keyed on the ARTIST rather than on where the music came from — so the same fetched bio serves a NAS FLAC, an Apple Music album, and Tidal later. Tom's requirement: bios are needed for local playback too, not only for Apple Music.

THE CHAIN: artist name → MusicBrainz mbid → external ids → Discogs, else Wikipedia, else Last.fm. Order chosen by Tom on measured evidence.

WHY NOT ROON'S SOURCE. Roon licenses TiVo/Rovi (AllMusic) — a commercial contract, not an API key. MusicBrainz returns the AllMusic artist id for free alongside the others, so if that licence were ever bought it is a swap at the last step of the chain and nothing else changes.

LAST.FM IS A STALE WIKIPEDIA FORK, which is why it is last despite having the longest text. Its Pat Metheny bio still says he "is ... leader of the Pat Metheny Group", a band that ended in 2010, where Wikipedia says "was ... (1977-2010)". Some of its entries are not biographies at all — one came back as a forty-line discography under a German heading.

COVERAGE MEASURED, characters after cleanup — nothing dominates, which is why it is layered:
  Pat Metheny    discogs 2669  wiki 468  lastfm 8482
  Vanessa Daou   discogs  148  wiki 365  lastfm 8684
  Kenny Wheeler  discogs  183  wiki 495  lastfm 1336
  Julia Hulsmann discogs  516  wiki 166  lastfm   90

ONLY GOOD BIOS ARE CACHED. Tom: "i don't like the idea of storing the lesser of a bio." Discogs and Wikipedia results are stored in artist_metadata keyed on mbid (v28); a Last.fm fallback is shown and never written, so the next visit retries the better sources and upgrades itself. One unlucky fetch during a Discogs hiccup cannot decide an artist's biography permanently.

TRAPS, all measured and all in the code comments: MusicBrainz must be queried with a PLAIN term — artist:"Eberhard Weber" returns nothing while Eberhard Weber returns him at 100; the exact name must beat a higher score, because Pat Metheny, Pat Metheny Group and Pat Metheny Trio are three different artists; and HTTP status codes must be checked, because a MusicBrainz 503 parsed as JSON becomes a silent "no biography".

NOT DONE: local artist pages have nowhere to show this yet — ArtistsView goes straight to an artist's albums. That screen is the remaining work for the local half of the requirement.

features.name: Zones become endpoints — the phone, Bluesound, AirPlay
features.desc:
AGREED IN PRINCIPLE 2026-08-21, unbuilt. Tom's ask: play on the phone itself, and have other endpoint types appear as zones when they are available.

THE ABSTRACTION ALREADY EXISTS AND THE VIEWS NEVER ADOPTED IT. AudioEndpointDriver is a protocol over execute/state/discoverEndpoints whose own header says drivers "understand endpoint operations only — no music domain concepts", and EndpointKind already declares sonos, airPlay, local and blueOS. Only SonosEndpointDriver implements it. Meanwhile ZoneDiscoveryService publishes [SonosZone] and ZonesView, the zone picker and every "Play on..." path bind to that concrete type.

SO THE UNIT OF WORK IS NOT "ADD THE PHONE AS A ZONE". It is promoting the view layer from SonosZone to the endpoint abstraction that is already there. Do that once and the phone, Bluesound and AirPlay are drivers rather than three special cases. Bolting the phone in as a pseudo-Sonos zone is the version that needs re-engineering afterwards.

THREE PIECES, in increasing size:
  1. SonosZone carries fields a local endpoint cannot answer — host (an IPv4 address), groupMembers, isHDMI, capabilities — referenced 13 times in ZonesView alone.
